💡 Key Takeaways

  • In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks.
  • Sources indicate that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Sources indicate that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

According to recent reports, I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Said topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Recent findings suggest that meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

Recent findings suggest that the French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for Latest Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

According to recent reports, as the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

It has been revealed that I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Sources indicate that there are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

The dessert course is about to go off with a perfect pumpkin pie, chocolate peanut butter pie, a caramelized onion tart, and more.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

Sources indicate that we love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

It has been revealed that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor.

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development.

The only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a major hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

It has been revealed that “We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the New York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Anna Theoktisto, Southern Living.

This zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the New York Times.

Sources indicate that I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

According to recent reports, I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who states that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Josh Walker & Duolan Li, Bon Appétit.

Tech Report: The Best Cast-Iron Skillets for a Lifetime of Cooking (2026)

📅 16 Jun 2021 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet.
  • There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.
  • To these two camps of people I say: “ I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some people there isn’t much of a debate around who makes the best cast-iron skillet. There is a diehard fanbase, loyal to the affordable, USA–made Lodge cast-iron pan, that will not hear of any other suggestions.

There are others (cast-iron nerds and collectors) who swear by the superior quality of their vintage pan from Griswold or Wagner that they found at a scrap yard, de-rusted in a bucket with a DIY electrolysis setup, and seasoned with a proprietary oil blend in the furnaces of their bespoke restoration workshop.

To these two camps of people I say: “ I don’t want to fight you, and I already know why you feel the way you feel. Please do not send me any angry emails.”.

Industry observers note that if you’ve been loyal to your own cast-iron pan for years—or decades—I don’t expect to change your mind. My goal is merely to provide recommendations for cast-iron cookware based on side-by-side testing and the input collectively provided by members of our staff. Agree with me and my team or don’t, either way, I'm happy if people are passionate about cooking with cast iron because I too enjoy it a great deal.

Cast-iron frying pans were the original nonstick pans, before ceramic nonstick and PTFE rolled around, and unlike modern nonstick coatings, a cast-iron pan’s surface actually gets more nonstick over time rather than degrading week by week. This is because, through continued cooking, thin layers of oil polymerize to the surface of the pan, creating a glassy nonstick surface that improves with continued use. They are also strong enough to handle metal utensils. The same can’t be said for that Instagram-famous nonstick pan (you know the one).

Sources indicate that yes, there are ways you can damage this seasoning layer, but these pans are far more resilient than lots of people think and they aren’t actually all that difficult to care for. Talk to cast-iron enthusiasts and they’ll tell you the best way to season a cast-iron skillet is to just keep cooking with it.

Sources indicate that and cook with it you can. Cast-iron pans are amazing for fried eggs, skillet hashes, cornbread, and sautéed greens. At a high heat, they do an incredible job searing strip steaks, London broil, and chicken thighs, giving you a crispy, burnished exterior.

Bottom line, cast-iron cooking is an absolute joy, and every kitchen tool kit should include some cast-iron alongside their stainless steel, carbon steel, and enameled Dutch ovens.

Newly introduced in this update: A review of Made In's new cast-iron pan, as well as more long term testing information for our winner.

Size(s): 10.5" (4.5 lb.), 12" (6 lb.), 13.5" (7.5 lb.)Preseasoned: Yes.

Sources indicate that what I loved: Because they're much more expensive than the Lodges folks got used to, many feel a certain type of way about the new era of smooth, vintage-style cast-iron pans that includes this Lancaster. But when you have the opportunity to test a bunch of these pans side by side, you really get a sense of their differences (however small), and you’d be surprised by the things you notice. It was in this apples-to-apples testing that this pan, manufactured by a small tech giant based in southeastern Pennsylvania, really set itself apart.

Industry observers note that the Lancaster is the lightest cast-iron pan I’ve tested, weighing in at 4 pounds for the No. 8 (10"-diameter) pan. Most cast-iron pans of a similar size are around 5 pounds or more—a seemingly small difference in number that makes a surprisingly big difference in hand. When laid out next to a dozen pans in the Test Kitchen, multiple testers singled out this pan as being the most comfortable to hold and maneuver.

Sources indicate that it has thinner walls than a typical cast-iron skillet, which allows it to heat up faster. In testing, it came to temp over one minute faster than pans with thicker walls. We were concerned this would mean a reduction in the level of heat retention you’d want to crisp up the edges of some skillet cornbread, but we didn’t find that to be a problem at all. The cooking surface also demonstrated relatively even heat for a cast-iron pan (you really can’t expect too much from cast iron though; cold spots are sort of inevitable with the material).

The pan comes preseasoned, but as is the case with most smooth cast-iron pans, this seasoning layer isn’t nearly as robust as what you’d find on a conventional Lodge or Victoria pan. The polished surface does aid in the pan’s nonstick properties though, so we found the pan was exceptionally nonstick right out of the box.

Sources indicate that other testing sites have criticized this style of smooth cast-iron pan for getting stained after cooking, but to that we say: This is the process of seasoning developing on the pan. That staining is a feature, not a bug.

An earlier design of this pan didn’t include a helper handle, a feature we missed but forgave because the pan was already so easy to wield. However, Lancaster recently updated the design to include one—all the better in our book. Check out my full review of the Lancaster No. 8 here.

It has been revealed that what I’d leave: The main drawback here is the cost. This pan will set you back $175, a steep price for cookware with a reputation for being budget-friendly. I'll just say this: People happily pay comparable prices for nonstick ceramic cookware that lasts only a year or two at best. This pan, provided you don’t drop it in an industrial crucible, will last a lifetime.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I have more patience than a lot of people when it comes to taking care of pans. So I will concede that the out of the box seasoning isn't that robust. Some tasks, like searing off meat, can strip the seasoning slightly at first. With the Lancaster, I've found that this doesn't impact the pans overall nonstick-ness. It does, however, mean you have to keep an eye out for rust until it gets a couple uses under its belt.

Recent findings suggest that below you'll see two Lancaster pans. The left is four years old and the right is fresh from the box (you can tell because the earlier generation of pans didn't have the helper handle). These are the pans after searing off two chicken thighs. You can see how the pan on the left has a robust, established seasoning, while the one on the right has some grey patches where the chicken skin pulled off some of that seasoning. From experience (I am the owner of the pan on the left), I can say that all you really need to do is keep cooking with it to get that seasoning back, but if you want to do a whole round of seasoning in the oven yourself, it certainly won't hurt. Honestly, had I just sautéed some onions in the rendered schmaltz after cooking the chicken, those spots would be taken care of.

For comparison, I seared some chicken thighs in both pans. The factory seasoning might get patchy after the first use. Don't let that scare you, just keep cooking with it. If you're really worried about rust, just wipe down the surface of the pan with a tiny bit of neutral oil, buff the excess off, and put it over the heat for a few minutes.

Sources indicate that some people complain about the cosmetic changes to these smooth pans when breaking them in To reiterate: It does not impact the performance of the pan. If it bothers you, I encourage you to think about how it's a record of use, and proof that it's growing and developing alongside you. Or, if you're just an unsentimental aesthete, perhaps read up on the concept of wabi-sabi. I personally think that my pan is the most beautiful piece of cookware I own!

If you want a high-quality pan that’s not only a pleasure to cook with, but can serve as a family heirloom for generations to come, consider this one. If you’re just looking for a workhorse that won’t break the bank, go for the budget option below.

Size(s): 4.8" (1.1 lb.), 6.5" (2 lb.), 8" (3.1 lb.), 10" (5.5 lb.), 12" (7.5 lb.)Preseasoned: Yes.

In a recent development, what I loved: Again, I apologize for snubbing Lodge, as even in our office we have a number of staunch brand loyalists. But in my testing, the Victoria edged out the fan favorite on two separate metrics. Victoria pans are preseasoned with flaxseed oil, and arrive glossy and exceptionally nonstick. Having a more thorough preseasoning is more key on cast-iron pans, as they are prone to sticking early on. We found the Victoria pan’s factory seasoning slicker than Lodge’s, which made frying potatoes and eggs ever so slightly easier. Do all cast-iron seasonings improve with continued use over time? Yes. But we know that some people want as much of a head start as they can get, and this pan offers you the best one.

The other way the Victoria bested the Lodge is in its form factor. The pour spouts on the Victoria are nice and wide, making it easy to pour off oil or other pan juices, and testers found the handle shape slightly more comfortable than the Lodge.

I'll be honest, though, these differences are pretty small, and if you feel drawn to the Lodge name, I recommend it as well.

Recent findings suggest that what I’d leave: Given it’s bargain pricing, there isn’t much to dislike here. I will note this pan is significantly heavier than the Lancaster pan—a full pound and a half for the same diameter skillet. Heavier skillets are cheaper and easier to produce, so it's a trade off you'll have to accept if you want a less expensive piece of cookware.

According to recent reports, 1. We had several members of staff handle the pans to get a broad sense of how easy the pans were to maneuver. Then we got to cooking.

2. Using a little bit of oil, we fried eggs sunny-side up and scrambled to see how much (if anything) stuck to the pan.

According to recent reports, 3. We seared skin-on chicken thighs to get a sense of how evenly heat was distributed around the cooking surface. We also measured how long it took for the pan to reach 375° at medium heat.

4. We washed the pans in hot water, noting any places where seasoning might have worn away.

Sources indicate that 5. We re-seasoned the pans ourselves in an oven for an hour at 500°.

6. We cooked another round of eggs to observe any changes.

Sources indicate that I omitted enameled cast-iron skillets like those made by Le Creuset or Staub because enameled surfaces offer a different experience in terms of both cooking and care. I also chose to exclude any cast-iron griddles or grill pans since they are too different functionally.

Sizing is a bit different from manufacturer to company, but I chose to stick with a 10"-diameter skillet—a No. 8 in traditional cast-iron sizing—as it is the most common size available.

How nonstick is the pan out of the box?

Recent findings suggest that I should clarify that cast-iron pans aren’t nonstick in the sense that you can cook an egg in the pan without any oil and slide it around. A really well-seasoned pan that’s a glossy lacquered black from years of use might get close, but the seasoning really just helps food release more easily from the pan—and the more seasoning there is, the less oil you’ll need for food to release.

I evaluated the pans on their out-of-the-box factory seasoning, because having a solid seasoning layer to start with diminishes the amount of time you need to break in a pan. This matters more with cheaper, rough textured cast iron, which is more prone to sticking when it lacks proper seasoning. For polished or vintage-style cast-iron pans (like the Lancaster), factory seasoning is nice, but the smooth surface also aids in preventing sticking, so it isn’t as crucial in the beginning stages of using the pan. That is why, throughout this review you see more emphasis on factory seasoning when discussing budget pans.

Is the pan designed in a way that makes it easy to use?

I counted form and design heavily in how I judged these pans. I wanted the pan to be comfortable and easy to maneuver, so I looked for pans that were lightweight (relatively, we're talking about iron here) and had handles that were comfortable to grip. If the pan was heavier, I wanted a helper handle for moving it from the cooktop to the oven. I didn’t place an emphasis on whether handle was designed to stay cool, because even a handle billed as “stay cool” will get dangerously hot when cooking for long enough, so I feel it’s better to just make a habit of always using an oven mitt or cloth to grab a cast-iron handle.

Recent findings suggest that heavy-duty, even-heating, satisfyingly weighty skillets are staples in the BA Test Kitchen because of their versatility. Stainless-steel and carbon-steel frying pans get hot swiftly, but they don't always have the heat retention capabilities of cast iron. And while nonstick pans are nice for scrambled eggs and crispy-skinned fish, many are not oven-safe and should never be exposed to high temperatures, so you can’t sear with them safely.

Stargazer Cast Iron Skillet - 10.5".

The Stargazer is a lovely pan. Like the Lancaster, its a vintage-style skillet, so it has a smooth texture that’s easy to clean. The surface develops seasoning well, and the curved lip allows for easy pouring at any angle. Ultimately, it is one of the heavier high-end skillets available on the market, which is why we don't have it as a winner, however if weight isn't a huge concern for you it is still an excellent pan.

According to recent reports, if you know cast-iron pans, you might see the Yeti cast-iron skillet and might find that it looks somewhat familiar. This is because Yeti acquired cult-favorite Butter Pat several years ago. The Yeti skillet is just the Butter Pat by a upcoming name, and apart from the logo, the finish, handle shape, and overall design remain unchanged. This pan has a nice velvety surface that holds on to seasoning very well, while still maintaining a smooth, glossier finish that makes vintage-style pans so desirable. Small gripes: The handle design wasn’t a favorite among testers, and the side walls are a slightly shorter than most other cast pans. It’s also a touch heavier, and a couple touches more expensive than our winner. Still, this is an excellent cast-iron pan and makes a great family heirloom.

Lodge Cast Iron Skillet with Red Mini Silicone Hot Handle Holder, 8-inch.

It has been revealed that people who track recommendations like these tend to be shocked that we don’t place the Lodge as our winner or budget pick. It is a fantastic pan, make no mistake. It has a great factory seasoning that’s resilient from the jump, and the 10" costs around 20 bucks—so what gives? When it came down to it, the Victoria pan had a slicker factory seasoning out of the box and a more comfortable handle design.

Recent findings suggest that smithey No. 10 Cast-Iron Skillet.

Another high-end polished cast-iron pan on the list. Smithey pans are gorgeous, so much so that it almost feels wrong cooking with them. However, you should cook with it straight away, as the factory seasoning is a little light on these, and we observed a little bit wearing away after the first couple rounds of cooking prior to us adding an additional layer of seasoning. Senior editor Noah Kaufman has been cooking with the Smithey multiple times a week for a couple years and says that within a few months of regular use and two bouts of seasoning in the oven he no longer worried about stuck eggs or steaks.

Gorgeous as they are, Smithey pans are heavy though, 5.8 lb. for the 10" skillet.

This skillet is the second lightest (4.3 lb. at 10") and has a velvety surface that holds on to seasoning a little better than the smooth polished pans. Like the Stargazer, it also has a curved lip instead of a pour spout, but I found that this pan does have a bit of a dribbling problem, which I wasn't crazy about. Still, one member of our team who has now lived with this pan for years loves it and uses it every day.

Lodge Cast-Iron Blacklock Skillet, Triple Seasoned - 10.25".

Lodge released this pan in response to the wave of latest and fancy polished pans, and as beautiful (quite beautiful), well-seasoned (three glossy layers), and lightweight as it is (almost even with the Lancaster), our testers found the handle uncomfortable to hold.

Sources indicate that ooni is a pizza oven company, and this pan is really designed for cooking in an oven rather than on the stovetop. It has a detachable handle, which is actually a genius bit of design that makes it easy and comfortable to grab out of a blazing hot pizza oven. But the sides are too shallow for doing more normal cast-iron things like frying chicken or sautéing greens. It is, however, great for cornbread and pizookies.

Industry observers note that this is Made In's official entry into the cast-iron new wave. The pan has a smooth machined surface, nice design touches, like curved sidewalls. and a spacious helper handle. The primary handle is nice to hold, however, a longer handle can make a pan feel heavier and add strain on the wrists. This pan is not the lightest either. I found it difficult to transport the full pan from the stovetop to the oven using only one hand, so consider this a pan for people with meaty forearms. Made In also uses flaxseed oil for the factory seasoning, which is a controversial choice in the cast-iron world. The reason for that controversy is that, while the finish flaxseed oil produces is glossy and attractive, it tends to be brittle. Especially with newer pans, a flaxseed seasoning has a tendency to wear away with regular cooking. After testing, I did notice this pan had some grey (unseasoned) patches after a round of searing meat. Again, not a massive deal—just keep cooking with it— but something to keep in mind. All of that being remarked I do still think this is a high quality pan. During the cooking tests, I had absolutely no issues with sticking whatsoever.

This pan is pretty similar to a standard Lodge or Victoria, but with a seasoning that’s not as nonstick out of the box. We did find, however, that it added latest layers of seasoning quite well.

Valor Preseasoned Cast-Iron Skillet.

In a recent development, the Valor is apparently a favorite in restaurants, but there’s nothing special to it that makes it stand out. If anything, the pour spouts are so small they might as well not be there at all.

It has been revealed that we’re all for innovation, which is what Finex sought to do with its octagonal pan and its bulbous handle, but we didn’t really observe any value from the modifications. While the octagonal shape is easier for flipping you could just use a bigger cast-iron pan for anything you want to flip. And its “speed cool” handle was awkward to hold.

Anytime KitchenAid ventures beyond the small appliance space you never quite know what you’re gonna get. In this case, it’s a cast-iron pan that is totally average in every way, except for its modern, minimalist design. We think this pan is too expensive for what you’re getting.

“Ooh, a lid!” Was the universal reaction to this cast-iron pan. If you like the idea of having a lid for your pan, then this is your pan. The problem with cast-iron lids, though, is that they don’t benefit from the progressive seasoning development the rest of the pan gets as you cook with it. Lids are only really dealing with evaporative moisture, which makes them even more likely to rust. Smithey, up above, sells glass lids that fit their pans, which, while not as oven safe, won't have that rust problem.

This is Victoria’s answer to the high-end polished cast-iron pan. The seasoning is great, but the pan is heavier than the Lancaster, and we didn’t love all the extra design embellishments. The brass insert on the handle had no practical value (it heated up quicker than the surrounding cast iron). Also all the extra ridges and divots just meant more places for gunk to get stuck in.

Recent findings suggest that amazon customers really like this pan. It comes with a silicone handle cover and a glass lid, which is nice (glass is a better material for a lid than cast iron). It also has tall 3" sides that make this pan great for frying. Beyond that, though, the pan is heavy and seemed to be barely preseasoned.

This is a super polished cast-iron pan with a glossy cooking surface that was nice to work with. However, we noticed quite a few cosmetic challenges, like small nicks and rough edges that made it seem like there were some corners cut in the manufacturing process.

Industry observers note that another pan that is just fine. The factory seasoning is minimal, so you’ll have to build that up yourself. There are several better options that are just as affordable from Victoria, Lodge, and others.

This is an affordable pan that looks a lot like a Lodge, but with a lesser factory seasoning.

Amazon Basics Preseasoned Cast-Iron Pan.

In a recent development, the seasoning that came on this pan out of the box was pretty bad, and with so many other cheap alternatives that offer much better quality, we don’t see the point in purchasing this pan. It’s also only available in a 15" diameter at the time of writing, which is bigger (and heavier) than most people need.

In a recent development, when you first get your pan, you’ll want to season it. We recommend this even when the pan comes labeled as preseasoned. To do this, just lightly rub a bone-dry pan with a thin layer of high-heat, neutral vegetable oil and place it upside down in a very hot oven—450°F–500°F should do the trick. Leave for an hour, turn off the heat, let it cool completely in the oven (you should be able to take it out without an oven mitt or towel), rub with a tiny bit more oil, and store. You can season cast iron as many times as you’d like to build up a glossy nonstick surface; when the pan looks dull or dry, it’s time to moisturize.

It has been revealed that no, you can’t chuck it in the dishwasher, and you won’t be using your normal hand-wash methods, but a cast-iron skillet really doesn’t require much love. When it’s time to clean up, simply wipe a damp rag across the surface of your pan, then dry it thoroughly. Often, that’ll be enough. But if there are any crusty bits, try pouring coarse salt in there and going at it with a Tawashi scrubber, which has soft bristles that whisk away any detritus. Many will tell you to avoid soap at all costs lest you ruin your careful seasoning, but a little dish soap is fine—just don’t let it sit in hot water. (Read our complete guide to cleaning cast iron.).

Industry observers note that for really baked on crumbs, try The Ringer, a handy chain mail scrubber that easily rinses clean between uses. After cleaning your cast iron, be sure to wipe your fry pan very dry—this is key for preventing any rust spots. Then take a teeny bit of neutral cooking oil (like canola or vegetable), smear on a paper towel, and give it a light coating. Take care to get the handle and the bottom as well as the cooking surface, as rust can crop up anywhere. And you’re good to go! It sounds involved, but it really only takes a few minutes. A well-seasoned pan takes virtually no time at all, so dutifully season and you’ll be rewarded.

Tossed your skillet in the sink absentmindedly or left it out in the rain only to find it’s developed a layer of orange rust? Don’t panic—rusting can happen pretty easily if you allow your pan to come into contact with water for an extended period of time (it is made of iron, after all). But that doesn’t mean it’s ruined. A salt scrub will help with most small spots, while a vinegar soak is the cure for more serious cases. (Read more on dealing with pesky cast-iron rust patches.).

If, after all of that, you’re still intimidated by raw cast-iron cookware, you might want to consider an enameled cast-iron skillet. It offers all of the heat retention and distribution of a well-seasoned cast-iron pan, plus it has a porcelain enamel to prevent rusting. Unlike a Le Creuset Dutch oven, enameled cast-iron skillets, like Staub’s, have a dark textured enamel that helps with browning and crisping.

According to recent reports, wilder Davies: I have been Epicurious and Bon Appétit's resident cookware tester and researcher for over 6 years. I have cooked with hundreds and hundreds of pans, and have asked chefs, materials scientists, and manufacturers far too many questions about things that go clank in the kitchen. I am a significant apologist of nonstick alternatives, and strongly believe in a buy-it-for-life ethos when it comes to outfitting your pantry.

Accor is paying up to own its fastest-growing business outright rather than list it now. The valuation is more than double what Ennismore was worth four years ago.

Accor has agreed to pay about €1.6 billion ($1.76 billion) to buy out minority investors, including co-founder Sharan Pasricha and Q Lifestyle Manufacturer, in Ennismore, its luxury lifestyle joint venture.

The deal, unveiled, Tuesday values Ennismore's equity at about €3.7 billion ($4.07 billion).

The Paris-based group plans to buy a combined 44.3% of Ennismore’s fully diluted share capital in three stages: 25.4% by the end of January 2027, another 6.3% by July 2027, and 12.6% by January 2028.

The announcement didn't specify Accor’s final expected ownership percentage. As of last month, Accor said it owns about 62.

Sources indicate that yasaman* is one of the regulars on Iranshahr, the fresh fashion hub of Tehran. Most evenings, she sets up a stall on the pavement and sells her drawings of manga and anime characters. On social media, she sports her own manga-inspired look: pink hair, pink mouth and smudgy pink eyeshadow extending beyond the corner of each eye. She tells her followers that, before she leaves her house, her mother claims: ‘Put on less makeup.’ ‘Mum, be reasonable,’ she answers. ‘I’m going to Iranshahr. For Iranshahr this is nothing. I’m going to Paris Fashion Week. You know everyone there is doing a catwalk.’.

Recent findings suggest that iranshahr’s sidewalks teem with young people parading the latest fashions and filming other young, stylish people for their social media feeds. This is where the fashionistas congregate, hanging out in cafés and galleries, and mingling on the sidewalks. Barely a headscarf is visible. The streets looked nothing like this a few years ago, but once the American-Israeli attacks began in February this year, the Islamic Republic has been fighting for its survival: with much of its leadership killed, the Strait of Hormuz under siege, and many of the country’s neighbours in league with the enemy, policing what people wear has slipped a long way down its list of priorities.

Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty Images.

The hijab law has been codified in Iran since 1983, enforced nationwide by the ‘morality’ police. Disobeying it meant fines, flogging or imprisonment. But then one act of disobedience changed everything. In December 2017, Vida Movahed, a woman in her 30s, climbed onto a utility box on Enghelab Street in Tehran, took off her white headscarf and held it up on a stick. Although she was arrested and later sentenced to a year in prison, her action proved contagious. Other women climbed up onto boxes and makeshift plinths in the same street, waving their headscarves in the air. People began calling them the Girls of Enghelab Street. They were arrested too. It is hard to convey now how much nerve their actions took. Women had been edging their scarves back for years, but taking one off in daylight, above the traffic, where the police could see their naked heads as clearly as everyone else, was something very few women had done in public, since the protests of 1979 and 1980.

Then, in September 2022, Mahsa Jina Amini died in custody of the morality police. Unlike the women on the boxes, she was not an activist: aged 22, a Kurdish woman visiting from Saqqez, a city 600 km west of Tehran, she’d been stopped because her loose headscarf was not covering enough of her hair. Her death brought thousands of people out on to the street in an outpouring of grief and anger. Women burned their headscarves. Cut their hair in front of cameras. Their protests spawned the Woman, Life, Freedom movement, and continued for months. What began as a demand for justice for one woman became a challenge to the compulsory hijab, then to the system itself. The authorities responded with arrests, executions and a repression that has never really stopped. The funerals of the dead became protests in their turn.

It has been revealed that what changed was that the morality police largely disappeared from the streets for months afterwards, with no announcement that the patrols had ended. Women who had grown up expecting to be stopped were not being stopped, and they knew why: the government had learned in 2022 what a single arrest could cost.

Sources indicate that azadeh, a woman from Tehran, tells me that, during the 12-day war with Israel in June 2025, the city felt apocalyptic. After the US president Donald Trump posted that people in Tehran should get out of the city, they fled their homes, leaving everything behind, and the city emptied. Checkpoints multiplied as the government waited for an uprising that never came. But in the strange mood that settled on the city following the attacks, Azadeh noticed another change – a bargain that nobody signed: ‘The state began leaving people alone to live as they like, as long as they do not come out into the street about it.’.

‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together’.

According to recent reports, what is happening in Tehran now is the quiet discarding of rules that have governed daily life for decades. A few inches of visible hair used to be the whole argument, but it is no longer the point. Women up and down the city are removing their scarves and manteaus – the loose, knee-length coats they were required to wear over their clothes in public – and adopting the latest trends: capri trousers, cropped and close-fitting clothes, bare arms, midi skirts, bare legs. Enjoying this new freedom, they parade along Iranshahr (rather aptly, the street takes its name from the old Persian word for the land of the Iranians), where shops that used to sell manteaus and headscarves have switched to blouses and T-shirts.

Industry observers note that A young woman whom I’ll call Mina puts the shift in blunter terms. ‘It isn’t optional anymore,’ she said. ‘You cannot leave the house in ordinary clothes. You have to be put together.’ She does not wear a headscarf anymore, and nor does anyone she goes out with. On the streets where people go to be seen, she tells me, hardly anyone does. In Tehran, those who can afford it wear the latest designer clothing. But in small Iranian towns, local workshops turn out such good copies of the latest Parisian and Latest York trends that anyone can now dress head to toe in ‘Chanel’, whatever their class.

Sima, also from Tehran, claims that: ‘Among the women who dress freely there is a kind of solidarity. Nobody talks about it, but everyone feels it.’ Recalling the first time she removed her headscarf, Sima says: ‘I felt bald … I thought everyone was looking at me, and I kept checking.’ She was frightened, she told me, so she kept a headscarf in her bag ready to whip out if anything should happen. It took a while for the feeling to pass. Each time she went out, she saw more women without headscarves and that gave her heart. She knew that she was not alone.

Photo by Atta Kenare/AFP/Getty Images.

The easy read on these developments, especially outside Iran, is that this is defiance: using clothing as a weapon against the state. The framing is not entirely wrong, but it misses most of what is happening on the street, and the people living it do not describe what they are up to in this way. When I asked Mina if getting dressed felt like a political act, she paused, then noted no. ‘When I dress up, it’s only for myself,’ she told me. ‘I’m not doing some political act.’ So what is happening on Iranshahr?

According to recent reports, the Iranian sociologist Asef Bayat has spent years asking how ordinary people can change their societies in the absence of formal organisations or conventional political movements. In Life as Politics: How Ordinary People Change the Middle East (2010), he argues that they do it less by protesting than by simply living as they wish to, and in enough numbers and for long enough that the rules have to bend around them. Bayat’s name for what Sima, Mina and Azadeh are describing is ‘the art of presence’. It denotes ‘the courage and creativity to assert collective will in spite of all odds, to circumvent constraints, utilising what is available and discovering newly introduced spaces within which to make oneself heard, seen, felt, and realised.’ It is a form of soft power.

Recent findings suggest that the women filling the sidewalks of Iranshahr Street are just ordering coffee and adjusting their sunglasses for a friend’s camera. They never chant slogans. They just hang out and admire each other’s looks. Each person is doing nothing more dramatic than deciding what to wear out of the house. But when thousands of young people make the same decision, on the same stretch of pavement, evening after evening, for months, the arithmetic changes. A protest might be cleared in a night. But a government has a harder time dealing with thousands of people who simply go on living as they want.

On Iranshahr young people filled the street to see who had shown up and how they looked.

The morality police have not gone away, but their methods have changed. Stopping a woman in public is expensive now: as the Woman, Life, Freedom protests revealed, it can end in months of demonstration, so the pressure has moved away from individuals to the places where women gather, and to the phones in their hands. Over the summer, several of the best-known cafés on Iranshahr and Sanaei Street, another popular hangout spot in Tehran, were shut down on the orders of judicial and police officials. The reasons given for the closures included serving customers who were not wearing the hijab. At least 42 businesses were shuttered across the country in August, and more than 70 social media accounts were blocked or seized. Last year, Tehran’s police chief intimated that plainclothes officers were working inside cafés and at concerts.

In a recent development, however, the state has also learned that it doesn’t always need to be there: a woman who assumes the café she is sitting in is being watched behaves as though it is. Still, the pressure is lighter than the state would ideally like to exert. In September, one senior official complained that ‘war conditions’ were preventing the authorities from enforcing the hijab as fully as they wanted.

In a recent development, as soon as the American-Israeli attacks were rolled out in February 2026, the government moved to occupy public spaces, fearing another wave of Trump-inspired protests. Every evening, it organised demonstrations of its own supporters, mainly on Vali-Asr, a few blocks west of Iranshahr. Two versions of public life were thus running at once. The government was turning out crowds to show that the public was still with it, while on Iranshahr young people filled the street to see who had shown up and how they looked.

Industry observers note that hair sits at the crossroads of these two versions of public life. For decades, it was kept out of public view, a private fact turned into a legal obligation, but now it is on display everywhere and deliberately so. Why hair? Probably because it is the most visible sign of femininity in public. In January 1936, Reza Shah, founder of the last dynasty to rule Iran before the revolution of 1979, asked his wife Queen Tadj ol-Molouk and their daughters to appear unveiled in public. He had them photographed, unveiled and wearing Western clothes, and distributed the images around the country, while his police went into the streets and pulled the chador off any woman still wearing one.

Reza Shah’s wife Queen Tadj ol-Molouk and their daughters Shams and Ashraf participating in a public ceremony unveiled, 8 January 1936. Courtesy Wikipedia.

Iran’s clergy read the move as a direct challenge. Decades later, the revolution led by that same clergy made covering the hair compulsory. Hair became a political battlefield. Whichever government has held power this century, women’s hair and the streets they walk in have been where the Iranian state reveals how much control it still has, because it is the one measure of its power that everybody can see at a glance.

From late December 2025 and into 2026, political protests demanding the end of the government were put down with lethal force, while the street culture of Iranshahr went on. These are not two separate populations. The people I spoke to on Iranshahr had been in those protests themselves. Both crowds were defying the state, but in very different ways, and this difference is easier to see if you start by considering what a crowd actually is.

In Crowds and Power (1960), Elias Canetti argued that a crowd is born at a single moment he called ‘the discharge’:.

The protestors in what has been dubbed Tehran’s Crimson Winter were this kind of crowd. Their demonstrations started in the bazaars over the collapse of the currency and the rising price of everything, and within 12 days they had spread to more than 100 cities. Footage demonstrated the main protest growing by the hour, until one of Tehran’s longest boulevards was full, end to end. It may well have been the discharge Canetti describes, of a pressure, years in the building, finally exploding. In the lethal crackdown that followed, human rights monitors verified 7,007 deaths, though some estimates put the toll at more than 30,000.

Industry observers note that the Islamic Republic has always tried to control its image and, above all, the image of its own power. What slips out of its hands can be tidied away, as long as nobody is looking. A crowd spreading across the country and shouting that the government must go cannot be tidied away. And so the government must clear the streets to prove its power still has reach.

Repealing compulsory hijabs would be a declaration of defeat, so the law stays on the books, unenforced.

Industry observers note that the Iranshahr collective is a crowd too, but it is not doing what the winter crowd did. Nobody on Iranshahr is asking the government for anything. Instead, they defy its authority by living in a way it cannot accommodate, but which is quieter and slower and much harder to suppress. This is where Bayat’s idea of the non-movement becomes useful. ‘What you are describing in the streets of Tehran might be explained in terms of non-movement, in the sense that these young people are displaying a kind of lifestyle that defies dominant norms, and in the case of Iran, even unwritten laws,’ he wrote to me.

In his book, Bayat defines non-movements as ‘the collective actions of noncollective actors’. It’s largely a question of conscious intent: ‘In non-movements,’ he told me, ‘actors do not necessarily see their acts as deliberate defiance or resistance. What they aim for is the realisation of an alternative mode of being and doing things that stands counter to the dominant ones.’ Non-movements describe the fragmented, improvised activities of large numbers of ordinary people who are rarely guided by an ideology or a leadership, but that trigger social change all the same. Most of the people making the decision to show up and defy norms, would, as Mina did, describe their choices as personal.

The agency of non-movements ‘rests on the power of big numbers’, as Bayat writes, against which a state may find it lacks the means to reassert control. But more importantly, the non-movement is difficult to police because it offers ‘escapes, spaces, and uncontrolled holes … that can be filled and appropriated by ordinary actors.’ It is the very ordinariness of these small escapes that allows the non-movement to quietly accrete.

According to recent reports, the Iranian government made this discovery for itself recently. In 2023, the judiciary drafted a Hijab and Chastity bill that was later passed but never brought into force. Indeed, the Supreme National Security Council of Iran told the legislature not to implement it. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, who belongs to the reformist camp, admitted on state television that he had ‘many reservations’ about a law he would himself be responsible for promulgating. ‘We risk ruining a lot of things in society because of this law,’ he stated. What he was referring to was the erosion of social trust. Enforcing the law would have required people to report each other over the hijab. Friends and families would have turned on one another; a taxi driver who failed to report an uncovered passenger would be fined.

In Bayat’s terms, this is what change from below can look like. In response to women persistently removing the hijab, the government never admitted a defeat. Repealing the existing law on compulsory hijabs would be a declaration of defeat, so the law stays on the books, unenforced, and the enforcement moves to where the political costs are lesser. What is being protected is the image of a state still in charge. If religion was the real concern, as hardliners want it to be, the law would be enforced whatever the cost, but the priority now is the regime and its survival. That is why a woman who removes her headscarf yet indicates nothing about the government is left alone. For the people of Iran, there has been no single, formal victory of the kind that a movement delivers, and no date to mark it. But the change is there anyway, in a street that looks nothing like it did a few years ago.

The Islamic Republic will no doubt put on a show of strength from time to time, asserting itself with a padlock, a patrol or a gun, but then it will pull back when it meets with people’s ongoing resistance. Each time it pulls back, a little more of its authority is lost, until one day it may find out that it has become something other than it was.

* Some names have been changed for security reasons.

The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • Industry observers note that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

Industry observers note that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever latest ideas have been simmering since last year’s significant meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

In a recent development, stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

It has been revealed that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody states they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

In a recent development, while more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

In a recent development, this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be mentioned is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

5 Gilded Age Etiquette Rules That Would Shock Modern People

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mentalfloss

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 1969, the last spike of the Transcontinental Railroad was nailed into a rail line in Promontory, Utah, officially connecting the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads.
  • The period is known as the Gilded Age today, a name taken from Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warnerâs satirical novel of the same name.
  • Women of all social classes faced a wide range of strict expectations during the Gilded Age, most centered on modesty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1969, the last spike of the Transcontinental Railroad was nailed into a rail line in Promontory, Utah, officially connecting the Union Pacific and Central Pacific railroads. The decade that followed was marked by extraordinary corruption and inequality in the United States, as entrepreneurs made fortunes off the shipping industry and the underpaid laborers who made it run.Â.

The period is known as the Gilded Age today, a name taken from Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warnerâs satirical novel of the same name. But while political and economic corruption ran rampant at this time, those who benefitted most from it simultaneously followed strict behavioral standards and moral codes. Some of these behavioral imperatives might seem outlandishly strict today, but back then, they were key to upholding a complex social hierarchy.

Women of all social classes faced a wide range of strict expectations during the Gilded Age, most centered on modesty. One particularly tricky balancing act women had to perform at this time was keeping their skirts away from mud, which was no small task given the amount of manure, dirt, and vehicle exhaust found on the average Gilded Age city street. At the same time, they were expected to avoid showing too much of their ankles. This body part was not always considered scandalous, and in fact, many Victorian-era dresses revealed womenâs ankles, but by the time the Gilded Age rolled around, long dresses were all the rage and members of polite society were expected to bury their ankles under silk, chiffon, velvet, and brocade.

Table manners were a detailed business among the upper classes of the Gilded Age, and dinner party faux pas could easily reveal a personâs nouveau riche background. Knowing which utensil was to be used for which dish was of paramount importance, and one particular etiquette guide noted that green peas were only supposed to be eaten with forks, not knives, âno matter how dexterously the feat may be performed.â (Of course, all this occurred while 90% of families in the nation were living on less than $1,200 per year and often struggled to afford food.)Â.

These days, itâs generally forgivableâif frowned uponâto shoot a quick message to your host letting them know youâll be a bit late. But this was not the case during the Gilded Age. Arriving early was considered slightly rude, but arriving late was absolutely taboo. Most dinner parties started between 7:30 and 8:30 p.m., at which time guests would be ferried into the drawing room, where drinks would be served. This was a critical moment for guests to examine one another, for young women to speak to suitors, and for all manner of networking to occur. According to some Gilded Age etiquette guides, being late by more than 15 minutes was absolutely unacceptable and could bring ruin to oneâs social status.

Recent findings suggest that dressing was an intricate and loaded affair among the upper classes of the Gilded Age, and women would sometimes change up to four or five times a day. According to the 1891 guidebook Manners, Culture and Dress of the Best American Society, it was vitally important to dress properly for every mealâand part of that involved not dressing too well, depending on who you were. âNever dress above your station,â the book advised, claiming this could lead to âgreat evils, besides being proof of an utter want of taste.â It even suggested that hostesses should dress in subdued colors to avoid outshining their guests.Â.

Today, making a new friend can be as simple as asking to meet for coffee, but things were a bit more complicated in the 1870s.

In a recent development, calls, or home visits, were central to Gilded Age social systems. These visits generally lasted around 15 minutes and involved extremely strict rules that were different depending on the time, location, and reason for the call.Â The 1884 guidebook Our Department stated that hostesses were expected to meet callers immediately and stand when guests arrived, and that gentlemen should be presented to the hostess first during introductions. If two women were visiting, however, the younger ought to be presented first. If the person one was calling upon was not home, visitors would leave their personal cards in silver trays in the hall, and the person receiving the card would either send a card back or pay a visit of their ownâbut only if they wished to continue the relationship.Â If they did not wish to, they simply would not send a card or call, which could theoretically be seen as the Gilded Age version of ghosting.

According to recent reports, home is where the heart isâand for those who watched 2026's Sense and Sensibility, that likely means the English countryside. In contrast to the clean lines of adaptations past, the latest take on Jane Austen's beloved romance novel leans into the rugged terrainâand messy matters of the heart.

As location manager Ian Hutchinson notes, director Georgia Oakley's vision for the film was to "make it quite raw and quite natural," adding that "you can really get into the rustic side of things." Thankfully, you donât need a Regency inheritanceâor a heartbreak at the hands of John Willoughbyâto experience the extravagant estates and moody moorlands firsthand. Here are five real-life filming locations across England where you can yearn, frolic, and live out your own period-drama fantasies to the fullest.

Industry observers note that the sisters' story begins at Norland Park, which in nonfictional England is brought to life by two separate estates in Dorset. The exterior grounds are played by Parnham Park, a 139-acre historic estate featuring ancient forests, rose gardens, and a spring-fed lakeâa fitting backdrop for fostering a hopeless romantic like Marianne. Itâs easy to see why a landscape so serene would be painful to leave; from skipping stones in the fuchsia flower-framed pond to taking long walks across the manicured lawns, much of the early action unfolds across the pristine grounds.

It has been revealed that roughly 15 miles away, Kingston Russell House stood in for Norland Park's interior shots and main entrance, its baroque-style arched windows and white stone Georgian facade creating an immediate visual contrast against the earthy, modest Barton Cottage that defines the rest of the film. Visitors looking to live out their Jane Austen fantasy can explore the picturesque grounds of Parnham Park or book a stay within the guest wing of the actual Kingston Russell House to fully immerse themselves in the Dorset countryside.

When the Dashwood women are forced to leave their frilly family home, they find refuge in the modest, moorland charm of Barton Cottage. In reality, the production team transformed Ditsworthy Warren Houseâa dilapidated cottage nestled deep within Dartmoor National Park. Like any run-down abode amidst the moors, the stone structure needed some work before it could fully emulate Barton Cottage. For logistical filming reasons as well as the benefit of the once-wealthy fictional family, windows and a new door were added. Otherwise, the stormy skies, rolling hills, and overall secludedness did most of the heavy lifting when it came to the drama of the Dashwoods' new home. Like any National Park in the UK, nature and Willoughby lovers alike can frolic through the tall, oftentimes damp grasses, imagining what could have been (or at least getting their steps in).

Recent findings suggest that for the windswept coastal moments where the drama of the waves mirrors the mental states of the characters, the production headed to Mothecombe Beach on the south Devon coast. The silverâor rather, seafoam greenâlining of the Dashwood sisters' migration to Barton comes in the form of whimsical strolls along the nearby shoreline. While you probably wonât find Willoughby or Marianne at Mothecombe Beach, this privately owned stretch of sand has all the moody views that most likely caught your eye in the 2026 adaptation. A quaint path leading down to the surf is located near the mouth of the Erme Estuary, alongside a cozy teahouse for when the sea breeze gets the best of you.

There's no such thing as a free lunchâor countryside cottage. That's where Barton Parkâin real life, Broughton Castle in Oxfordshireâcomes in. As the price for their humble accommodations, the Dashwoods are frequently summoned to the 14th-century moated manor of their spirited landlord and cousin, Sir John Middleton. With its fortified gatehouse, armor-adorned Great Hall, and Tudor-era upgrades, the castle looks far more suited for fending off medieval sieges than hosting awkward Regency dinner parties. Today, travelers (and fans of The Crown and My Lady Jane, which also filmed at Broughton Castle) can cross the stone bridge over the moat to tour the historic rooms and manicured gardensâminus the obligation of amusing Mrs. Jennings.

Sources indicate that the Dashwood sisters experience all the emotions in Sense and Sensibilityâand seemingly every postcode in southern England while theyâre at it. Eventually, the drama sweeps them to London, brought to life by West Wycombe Park in Buckinghamshire. This 18th-century Palladian villa was constructed for a real-life DashwoodâSir Francisâand its lavishly decorated staterooms, marble walls, and cross-era architectural accents are now owned by the National Trust. Today, the estate opens to the public during the summer months, when hopeless romantics can spend the day staring at painted ceilings and strolling along the swan-shaped lake within its 45 acres of landscaped parkland.

Adani Group has signed deals with Indian Hotels Company and IHG Hotels & Resorts to build about 3,500 rooms across all eight of its airports, using land it already controls and leaving the hotel companies to run them.

The latest agreement, announced Oct. 29, brings together Adani Airport Holdings (AAHL) and Indian Hotels Firm (IHCL) to develop eight hotels with more than 2,000 rooms combined, across Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Lucknow and Guwahati.
