Tech Report: The Best Haunted Hotels to Book for a Spooky Getaway

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety.
  • At these hotels, lodges, inns, and resorts around the world, the supernatural is embraced and the unsettling is celebrated.
  • Prices shown are approximate starting rates for a standard double room per night, based on rates current as of September 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nothing beats staying in a hotel whose suites hold some stories — especially if they’re of the spooky variety. The same friends who roll their eyes at mentions of luxury amenities and amazing views will be wide-eyed when you tell them about the ghost you accidentally ate breakfast with, the wailings you heard on your way to the icebox, or your run-in with an uncanny Victorian woman wearing all black. Booking a room at a regular old hotel will give you a few nice photos and a comfy robe; booking a room at a haunted one will give you tales of terror to tell for the rest of your life.

At these hotels, lodges, inns, and resorts around the world, the supernatural is embraced and the unsettling is celebrated. Unexplained occurrences are simply part of the experience, and those with a healthy level of morbid curiosity will find no shortage of places to explore. Here, dark lore is hidden in every nook and cranny: a quack doctor’s treatment room, geothermal soaking pools, an old-school saloon, and a clown statue collection. Look over your shoulder and you might spot a glowing orb, a sopping-wet child, or a murderous outlaw. No matter where on this list you choose to book your stay, get ready to expect the unexpected.

Prices shown are approximate starting rates for a standard double room per night, based on rates current as of September 2026. Rates vary significantly by season — expect higher prices in October. USD figures for non-US properties are approximate conversions.

Recent findings suggest that pricing note: All rates are approximate starting prices for a standard double room, verified September 2026. Rates fluctuate significantly by season — October is the busiest and most expensive month at all of these properties. UK properties are priced in British pounds (£); USD equivalents are approximate. The Lodge at Hot Lake Springs books via Airbnb. Always confirm rates and availability directly with the property before booking.

Recent findings suggest that savannah has long been known for its thriving ghost population, many of whom have taken up residence at the city’s oldest hotel. Established in 1851 by Mary Magdalene Marshall, the building has played many roles: a makeshift hospital during the mid-19th-century yellow fever epidemic, a Union hospital near the end of the Civil War, and a temporary home to Joel Chandler Harris, creator of Uncle Remus, during the Reconstruction era. It’s no wonder then that guests frequently report odd activity in the hotel’s period-detailed rooms and cozy library. Common occurrences include the sound of children running down the halls at night, strange figures spotted in the foyers, doorknobs rattling, and faucets turning on on their own. Many Savannah ghost tours stop outside the hotel, but nothing beats drinking spirits amongst the spirits during the nightly social hour (sometimes with live entertainment!).

Sources indicate that for a long time, the Crescent Hotel seemed cursed: Just before it opened, in 1886, a stonemason working on the structure fell to his death and later, in the early 20th-century, a young woman may or may not have been pushed out of a top floor window. Eventually, the hotel landed in the hands of Norman Baker, a quack doctor who “treated” his mental patients using inhumane methods. (He was eventually arrested but only after plenty of damage was already done.) Needless to say, there are numerous rumors that now swirl around the hotel, with many visitors spotting doctors, nurses, and patients from the hospital roaming the corridors. Room 218, where the stonemason met his end, is considered the most haunted spot in the hotel, but most anywhere you venture you’ll find mysteries galore. The staff leads daily ghost tours — including a look at Baker’s old autopsy table in the basement — and there are even midnight ESP investigations for especially fearless guests.

Recent findings suggest that this rural Scottish inn on the edge of Loch Lomond is home to a colorful cast of spirits, including an entire family. Legend has it that this family got lost in the snow while looking for shelter, all of them freezing to death in the night. Now, in death, they’ve finally gotten their wish of a place to stay in room two at the inn. Meanwhile, down the hall in room six lives a little girl who supposedly drowned in the river behind the building. Guests staying in her room have, on occasion, seen her small figure dripping in water and have even felt her in the bed beside them. Last but not least, there’s Angus: a young cattle drover who was murdered by members of a rival clan and now screams in pain as he wanders the property for eternity. After you’ve greeted the ghosts, make sure to grab a pint from the inn’s bar and restaurant, where taxidermy animals, old china dishes, and exposed wooden beams transport you back in time. The most daring guests of all will not shy away from a heaping plate of haggis or a hefty helping of mince and tatties.

In a recent development, railroad tycoon Alex Johnson built this hotel in 1927 to attract high society to Mount Rushmore, the West’s newest tourist trap. Though he passed away in 1938, his dream came true: Over the years, the hotel hosted six U.S. presidents and even served as a temporary home for Alfred Hitchcock and Cary Grant during the filming of “North by Northwest.” It’s a testament to the grandeur of Hotel Alex Johnson that none of its famous guests were deterred by its more mysterious elements, i.e., the Lady in White who haunts the eighth floor. This bride supposedly jumped to her death while staying at the hotel on her wedding night, and now, guests wake up to her opening their windows and dresser drawers. If you don’t see the Lady in White, you might instead spot John himself, who still keeps an eye on day-to-day business with his young daughter by his side. For amateur ghost hunters, the hotel offers a ghost adventure package that includes lodging in a haunted room, a ghost detector, and other, less-haunted perks like a $25 dining credit and free valet parking.

Industry observers note that everything was going swimmingly for this hot springs resort until, in 1934, a raging fire destroyed half the building and put it out of business. In the years after, the space was used as a nurse’s training school, a retirement home, a restaurant, and an insane asylum; however, in 1991, it was entirely abandoned and left to the elements. During this 15-year offseason, many a story started to spread about The Lodge, such as it being haunted by (among others) a gardener who committed suicide on the property, a nurse who perished in the lake, and a number of asylum inmates. So dark did this once-grand establishment’s reputation become that it appeared on the ABC series “The Scariest Places on Earth” in 2001. Two years later, new owners cleaned up the building and reopened it to the public as a spa and B&B with geothermal soaking pools, a bar and restaurant, and a 60-seat movie theater. The Lodge is a bit reticent to discuss its dicey past, but guests still report odd figures in windows, random screams, and a piano playing itself.

Sources indicate that in its heyday, Gran Hotel Bolivar was the swankiest place to stay in all of Lima, welcoming politicians, artists, Hollywood stars, and rock legends. The Rolling Stones spent the night here (before being kicked out for poor behavior), while Ava Gardner once danced barefoot in the bar. Charles de Gaulle, Orson Welles, and Ernest Hemingway are just a few of the hotel’s many other renowned guests. However, by the time it was declared a national landmark in 1972, Gran Hotel was on the decline; latest, modern hotels pulled away business and its sketchy owner fled the country, leaving financial ruin in his wake. It was around this same time that ghost stories started to emerge, with “insiders” claiming that the hotel’s fifth and sixth floors were closed not (as reported) for financial reasons but because they were severely haunted by former guests and employees. Even on the floors that are still operational, ghosts have been mentioned to turn on and off the coffeemakers, radios, and televisions.

According to recent reports, back in the day, as Americans journeyed out west, this hotel offered weary travelers a place to rest their heads (and get a cold drink). Many outlaws like Wyatt Earp, Jesse James, Billy the Kid, and Buffalo Bill Cody stopped here on their way down the Santa Fe Trail, and thus (unsurprisingly), the inn became known for its frequent murders. (Supposedly, “Wonder who got killed at Lambert’s place this weekend?” was a common question around Cimarron.) With the exception of a modern annex, the hotel still looks much like it did in the days when drinking, gambling, and guns were the norm, with a creaky wooden staircase, deer antlers on the walls, and a big stone fireplace in the dining room. There’s only one bedroom that guests are unable to book: room 18, where T.J. Wright, infamous ne’er-do-well and onetime owner of the hotel, was killed by an unknown gunman. Doomed to the room for eternity, he does not take too kindly to visitors.

It has been revealed that with more than 600 years of history under its belt, it’s easy to see why this quaint inn is one of the world’s most haunted places to stay. Factor in that it was built shortly after French raiders burned all of Rye to the ground, and it’s no wonder there are some restless souls lingering around. The cellars beneath the inn date back all the way to the 12th century, and the secret tunnels connecting them were once used by smugglers from the notorious Hawkhurst Gang. In fact, many folks believe that members of the gang still use the tunnels today, even roaming upstairs to visit guests from time to time. The inn’s 31 rooms are all named after notable people from either Rye’s or the inn’s history, and a handful of them are also said to be haunted. Among the resident spirits are two 16th-century swordsmen, engaged in a perpetual duel in room 16, and the wife of gang leader Arthur Gray in room 17.

The self-proclaimed “birthplace of the American beach vacation” has wowed big-time guests for over a century. Marilyn Monroe, Charlie Chaplin, President Franklin D. Roosevelt, and L. Frank Baum all enjoyed its luxury suites and sandy beaches, surely reveling in the relative privacy afforded on a tidal island. The hotel has many claims to fame, from lighting up the world’s first outdoor electric Christmas tree, to being featured in the film “Some Like it Hot,” to — you guessed it — housing a famous ghost. In 1892, 24-year-old Kate Morgan checked into the hotel and never checked out, her body found on an exterior staircase with a gunshot wound to the head (which the coroner ruled a suicide). If you tire of Hotel Del’s luxury and want a bit more spook in your stay, take a walk past Kate’s room, where many odd phenomena have been reported. Guests and staff alike have recalled sudden cold breezes, phantom footsteps, and electronics turning on and off on their own. Some have even spotted a Victorian woman dressed in black wandering the halls or standing alone down at the seashore.

This eerily jolly roadside fully embraces its role as nightmare fodder, leaning into the common fear of clowns with horror-movie-themed rooms (all with a clown twist, of course). From “Friday the 13th” to “Chucky” to “Halloween,” the motel lets you choose which creepy world you wish to enter. Even the “normal,” non-movie rooms are a bit disconcerting, with strange clown wall art and plenty of ghosts. The cemetery right next to the motel is home to such distinguished residents as Bina Verrault, a conwoman from New York; Sheriff Thomas Logan, who was shot while investigating a local brothel; and Clarence David, the father of motel co-founders Leroy and Leona David. In fact, Clarence’s 150 clown statues formed the first of the Clown Motel’s collection, which has since expanded to over 4,000 pieces of clown memorabilia. In a 2015 episode of “Ghost Adventures,” host Zak Bagans and his crew explored the motel’s spiritual resonances and even captured on camera the hand of a large clown moving entirely of its own accord.

Just down the road from the Clown Motel, the Mizpah offers a completely different (but equally spooky) experience. Built in 1907, at the height of Tonopah’s silver boom, the hotel was long a hub for investors visiting from the east coast; however, as silver prospects slowly declined, the Mizpah floundered and ultimately closed its doors in 2000. After sitting abandoned for 11 years, it was purchased by the owners of several Sonoma wineries and restored to its former glory — a process that included capitalizing on its many spooky stories. Among the hotel’s undead residents are U.S. Senator Key Pittman (whose body was hidden in a bathtub full of ice within his suite) and the Lady in Red, a 1920s prostitute who was strangled by one of her clients on the fifth floor. At the front check-in desk, guests are encouraged to write about their encounters with the Lady in Red (or any of the other ghosts) in a dedicated notebook; some have even left photos of their supernatural experiences.

It was after a stay here, in room 217, that Stephen King dreamed up his 1977 horror masterpiece, “The Shining,” shaping the fictional Overlook Hotel in the mold of this mountainside retreat. In fact, early in the novel, room 217 is mentioned as a place that the clairvoyant son, Danny, must avoid under all circumstances. However, the Stanley was home to eerie activity long before King made it famous, with the story going that its founder, Freelan O. Stanley, still drifts through the lobby and billiards room from time to time. Guests have also heard children running and playing at odd hours, witnessed cupboard doors unlock and open on their own, and, in room 407, spotted a cowboy apparition (perhaps the spirit of local legend “Rocky Mountain Jim.”) The Stanley proudly embraces its haunted reputation: playing the 1980 film adaptation of “The Shining” on an endless loop on the hotel TVs and leading a number of different ghost tours all year long. There’s the classic Stanley ghost tour, a “Shining” tour, a seasonal Halloween tour, and even a one-of-a-kind Frozen Dead Guy tour (which is basically exactly what it sounds like).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there are few filmmakers who have turned their personal taste in movies into as recognizable a cinematic language as Quentin Tarantino. His films are all love letters to the movies he grew up watchingâbe they spaghetti Westerns, kung fu epics, exploitation cinema, or pulpy genre filmsâmany of which were movies that didnât usually receive much recognition from critics.Â.

Sure, he might borrow a lot of the ingredients, but he rearranges them into something thatâs distinctly his own, and often uses familiar genre conventions to explore the mythology of Hollywood.Â He also has a knack for making seemingly throwaway conversations feel as important as a shootout, and for turning a well-placed needle drop into an event in itself.

Tarantino's opinions about modern cinema may have become increasingly controversial in recent years, but the films themselves remain a formidable body of work. With his self-imposed ten-movie limit still hanging over him, it might be several more years until we see his final one. But this also makes it a good time to revisit his filmography to rank every one of his movies.Â.

Death Proof is Tarantino at his most deliberately âtrashy,â and that is both part of its appeal and maybe one of its limitations. It was made as part of the double feature Grindhouse alongside Robert Rodriguez's Planet Terror, and the film recreates the rough edges of exploitation cinema with its scratched prints, missing reels, and abrupt edits.

Recent findings suggest that the first half of the movie lures viewers into expecting the familiar rhythm of a 1970s slasher, with Mike (Kurt Russell) preying on a group of unsuspecting women. Then the second half subverts the trope and introduces a new group of women who are not helpless victims; theyâre physically capable and more than willing to turn the tables on Mike.Â.

Death Proof is probably the least good film in Tarantino's filmography, but even then, it's a very solid movie.

It has been revealed that tarantino considers Kill Bill to be one movie, much to the dismay of many fans. But fine, we'll indulge him. Both chapters are excellent, although Volume 1 has a slight edge thanks to the narrative excitement of the Bride's revenge missions.Â.

The film is a sprawling tribute to the cinema that shaped him, taking inspiration from Shaw Brothersâ kung fu movies, Japanese samurai films, spaghetti Westerns, and even a bit of anime. The influence of the Japanese revenge classic Lady Snowblood is especially noticeable.Â.

Volume 2, meanwhile, slows things down and has a bit more of a spaghetti Western vibe (with plenty of martial arts).Â.

Jackie Brown is probably Tarantino's most underrated film, partly because it arrived after Pulp Fiction and might not have lived up to those same expectations.Â.

Adapted from Elmore Leonard's novel Rum Punch, it trades in the elaborate criminal mythology of his previous movie for a more grounded story about a flight attendant (Pam Grier) trying to outsmart a dangerous gunrunner, along with the law enforcement agents watching him.Â.

The film is also a homage to blaxploitation cinema of the 1970s. The ensemble cast is exceptional, especially Robert De Niroâs performance as a miserable, increasingly frustrated ex-convict.Â.

Following Django Unchained, Tarantino returned to the Western genre with a pretty claustrophobic film. The Hateful Eight traps a collection of bounty hunters, fugitives, and strangers inside a Wyoming haberdashery during a blizzard.

Where Django Unchained is a grand adventure driven by liberation and revenge, this film is cynical and aggressively unpleasant. Its characters are rarely trustworthy, even the âprotagonists.â.

According to recent reports, the movie was shot in Ultra Panavision 70mm, a very wide format with a 2.76:1 aspect ratio that had largely disappeared from mainstream filmmaking at the time. The expansive landscapes surely look spectacular, but the wide frame also helps make the cramped interior scenes visually striking and allows several characters to fit in the same composition.

Ennio Morricone's score goes to great lengths to add a huge sense of dread and isolation, which won him his first competitive Academy Award for a film score. The third act gets a little messy and maybe reveals its hand a bit too soon, but the performances, cinematography, and music keep this a hugely entertaining Western.

Recent findings suggest that A debut feature film rarely showcases a filmmaker's defining style and personality as confidently as Reservoir Dogs did. Made on a modest budget, Tarantino's first movie follows a diamond heist that goes wrong, although the actual robbery is never shown.Â.

Industry observers note that instead, the film moves between the surviving criminals' warehouse hideout and flashbacks that slowly reveal how the operation fell apart. This narrative device tells viewers exactly what kind of storytelling Tarantino likesâthe mechanics of the crime matter less than the people and the air of suspicion involved, and the conversations that expose them. Who needs to see how the robbery went when the aftermath is this much more entertaining?

According to recent reports, the opening scene is also a perfect example of the filmmaker's approach to dialogue. The characters talk about everyday nonsense with the confidence of people who have known one another for years.

It has been revealed that calling Pulp Fiction Tarantino's magnum opus is hardly an original observation, but its reputation as a fan favorite is well deserved. The film takes a collection of Los Angeles crime stories and rearranges them into a nonlinear puzzle, and allows characters to disappear from the narrative only to return in unexpected places.Â.

Thanks to this, Vincent Vega can abruptly die in the middle of the story, and an encounter in a diner that occurs early in the film's chronology can become its final scene. The structure isnât all that easy to pull off, but the movie does it.Â.

Industry observers note that john Travolta's career-reviving performance as Vincent, Samuel L. Jackson's Jules, Uma Thurman's Mia, and Bruce Willis's increasingly desperate Butch form a cast that understands the film's rhythm instinctively.Â.

Other Tarantino films may surpass it in individual sequences or performances, but only some capture so many of its highs at once.Â.

Few Tarantino films contain as many scenes that could stand alone as masterclasses in sheer tension as Inglourious Basterds. Christoph Waltz's Landa is a major reason so many of these scenes work, but MÃ©lanie Laurent, Michael Fassbender, Diane Kruger, Brad Pitt, and the rest of the ensemble are equally memorable in their own ways.

Sources indicate that you might not realize that the film is around 70% non-English. German, French, and Italian are all naturally woven into the dialogue. The tavern sequence (with Michael Fassbenderâs character) is especially effective since the characters' ability to pass as someone they're not depends on getting small linguistic and cultural details right.

Instead of playing out like a standard World War II drama, the movie subverts expectations by letting the characters rewrite history in an explosive finale inside a movie theater, and ends on a fittingly high note.Â.

In a recent development, anyone expecting your usual fast-moving Tarantino movie might find Once Upon a Time in Hollywood surprisingly patient and tame in comparison. Much of the film follows actor Rick Dalton and his stunt double, Cliff Booth, through an ordinary stretch of life (and its mundane tasks) in late-1960s Los Angeles.Â.

Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt have terrific chemistry, with Rick's insecurity and Cliff's unshakable cool creating a friendship that feels genuine.Â.

The film's recreation of 1969 Hollywood is pretty detailed, from its billboards and radio broadcasts to the television indicates and movie theaters spread across the city.Â.

Just like with Inglourious Basterds, the movie eventually rejects the historical record in favor of a revisionist ending, turning the Manson family into the targets of a violent finale that completely pays off.Â.

Django Unchained is Tarantinoâs absolute best. Here, heâs operating with the confidence of a filmmaker who knows exactly how to make a scene land. Its story of a formerly enslaved man teaming up with a bounty hunter to rescue his wife from a plantation owner has the makings of a grand Western adventure, but the film's greatest scenes are often the individual encounters.Â.

The writing is also among Tarantino's strongest. The film also borrows heavily from the Italian Western tradition, beginning with Luis Bacalov's theme and drawing on the visual language of Sergio Corbucci's 1966 classic, Django.Â.

According to recent reports, its soundtrack is particularly interesting. Rather than having a traditional score, it combines older Western compositions with blues, soul, and even contemporary hip-hop. The modern tracks might seem an odd fit on paper, but they give the film an energy that fits with its revisionist approach to history.Â When "100 Black Coffins" starts playing, it's hard to imagine a more fitting choice.

Few movies have turned a familiar genre into such a wildly elevated narrative experience.

  • The pages traveled from Henleyâs Southern California barn to the writerâs home in Upcoming Yorkâs Hudson Valley, but the book went nowhere: Eagles manager Irving Azoff later testified that publishers made no offers and that he believed Glenn Frey ultimately killed the project.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Eaglesâ Hotel California turns 50 this December, and itâs still one of the biggest albums of 1976. Before the songs were finished, though, they existed on legal pads that Don Henley bought at a Los Angeles stationery store. Roughly 100 of those handwritten pages ended up at the center of a Manhattan criminal case that collapsed in the middle of the trial.

In a recent development, the pages left Henleyâs hands because of an authorized Eagles biography. Writer Ed Sanders started work on it in 1979, under a contract that said the band would furnish him material that would remain its âsole property,â and Henley let him sort through the lyric drafts for research.Â.

The pages traveled from Henleyâs Southern California barn to the writerâs home in Upcoming Yorkâs Hudson Valley, but the book went nowhere: Eagles manager Irving Azoff later testified that publishers made no offers and that he believed Glenn Frey ultimately killed the project.

Around 2005, Sanders sold the pages to rare-book dealer Glenn Horowitz, who later sold them to former Rock & Roll Hall of Fame curator Craig Inciardi and memorabilia auctioneer Edward Kosinski. Henley only realized the pages were missing when they highlighted up for sale, and in April 2012, according to the indictment, he paid Kosinski $8,500 for some of the âHotel Californiaâ sheets.Â.

In a recent development, over the years, the writer gave Horowitz several accounts of where the pages came from: Henleyâs assistant had sent them from Malibu, heâd found them discarded in a backstage dressing room, or someone who worked for the band had handed them over. âIt was about 35 years ago and my memory is foggy!â he wrote in 2012.

Industry observers note that by 2017, with Henleyâs lawyers and the Manhattan District Attorneyâs office both asking questions, Horowitz asked the writer whether the pages had come from Frey, who had died the year before. âOnce you identify GF as the source of the tablet, you and I are out of this picture for good,â Horowitz wrote in a follow-up, according to the indictment.Â.

It has been revealed that none of the three men was accused of stealing anything, but in July 2022 they were charged with conspiring to keep and sell pages they knew Henley considered stolen, which prosecutors valued at more than $1 million. âThey made up stories about the origin of the documents and their right to possess them so they could turn a profit,â DA Alvin Bragg mentioned. Kosinskiâs lawyer, Antonia Apps, called it âthe weakest criminal case I have seen in my entire career.â.

Sources indicate that the nonjury trial opened in February 2024 before Judge Curtis Farber, and Henley spent three days on the stand. âI always knew those lyrics were my property. I never gifted them or gave them to anybody to keep or sell,â he said. Then Henley and his lawyers waived attorney-client privilege, and about 6,000 pages of communications reached both sides within a few days. The defense said the emails indicated that Henley had first suspected someone else before being reminded of the book, and that some of his lawyers and a private investigator had called the disappearance a burglary, without mentioning Sandersâ contract, because they thought it would help their cause.

On March 6, 2024, prosecutors dropped the case. âThese delayed disclosures revealed relevant information that the defense should have had the opportunity to explore,â Assistant DA Aaron Ginandes told the court. Farber mentioned witnesses and their lawyers had used the privilege âto obfuscate and hide information that they believed would be damaging,â that prosecutors âwere apparently manipulated,â and that the DAâs team, âwhile eating a slice of humble pie, are displaying the highest level of integrity in moving to dismiss the charges.â.

Henleyâs lawyer promised a fight in civil court, and Henley sued to get the pages back. In November 2025, a judge threw out Horowitzâs malicious prosecution suit against Henley and Azoff, finding the DA had âample probable cause.â As of that ruling, the lyric sheets were still in the custody of the Manhattan DAâs office, waiting on a decision about who actually owns them.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The short answer to why theyâre called 7-Eleven is one Mental Floss has given before: the stores were open from 7 a.m.
  • It has been revealed that before home refrigerators, Texans bought block ice, and the Southland Ice Company sold it from retail docks around Dallas.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 1946, a Dallas ice organization that had stumbled into the grocery business decided its stores needed a new name, and it hired an advertising agency to come up with one.

The short answer to why theyâre called 7-Eleven is one Mental Floss has given before: the stores were open from 7 a.m. to 11 p.m. The longer answer starts with a man selling eggs off an ice dock.

It has been revealed that before home refrigerators, Texans bought block ice, and the Southland Ice Company sold it from retail docks around Dallas. In 1927, a dock operator named John Jefferson Green, known as Uncle Johnny, went to Joe C. âJodieâ Thompson, one of the companyâs founding directors, with a pitch: he wanted to sell milk, eggs, and bread alongside the ice. âYou furnish the items,â he suggested, âand Iâll pay the power bills.â Thompson agreed, and the company now bills that dock as the worldâs first convenience store.

The stores got their first name a year later. A Southland manager came home from a trip to Alaska with a souvenir totem pole and planted it outside his store, and it drew so much attention that employees suggested putting one at every dock and calling them Toteâm Stores, since customers toted their purchases away. Southland went for it. By 1939, the organization had 60 of them in the Dallas-Fort Worth area, and its executives were known as the â7-7-7 crowdâ for working from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m., seven days a week.

The hours came before the name did. By 1945, the stores were open from 7 in the morning to 11 at night, seven days a week, and that year the parent company reorganized as the Southland Corporation. In 1946, Southland hired the Dallas agency Tracy-Locke to rename the Toteâm stores, and the agency chose 7-Eleven to advertise the long hours. The company remodeled the stores at the same time and doubled their floor space.

It was a good shop to ask. A 2013 Texas House resolution honoring the agencyâs centennial credits it with Elsie the Cow for Borden in 1936, with coining the word âslacksâ for Haggar in 1940, and with introducing Doritos as a brand in 1966. Decades after naming 7-Eleven, the same shop ran the chainâs Simpsons Movie Kwik-E-Mart promotion in 2007.

The other thing people notice about the name is the logo, where every letter of âELEVENâ is a capital except the last one. Even 7-Elevenâs explanation is secondhand: the tech giant has said it is believed that the wife of its president in the 1960s found the all-caps version a little harsh and suggested a lowercase n to make the logo look more graceful.

Best Knife Set After Years of Testing Knives (2026)

📅 14 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3886 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task.
  • It has been revealed that after testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife.
  • It has been revealed that when it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’m just going to say it: You don’t need an 18-piece knife block with a blade for every conceivable kitchen task. If you find one of those sets out in the wild, what you’ll probably find is that a lot of knives in the block still have a factory-sharp edge, because they’ve never been used. At the same time, it’s hard to ignore the sheer value a lot of knife sets offer. For most home cooks, buying every knife piecemeal is akin to adding a 15%–20% tax.

It has been revealed that after testing dozens and dozens of knives and talking with our Test Kitchen editors and professional chefs, the consensus is that the best knife set really only needs three essentials: a chef’s knife, a bread knife, and a paring knife. As you get more confident or curious in the kitchen, you might choose to add a versatile nakiri knife, a handy petty knife, or a versatile cleaver, but we generally recommend doing so on an ad hoc basis with an eye for how it will fit into your cooking and how much you truly want to spend on a knife.

It has been revealed that when it comes to the core pieces of a knife set, though, many of the best knife makers make great versions of multiple knife types. In that spirit, the sets here offer high performance and great value without compromise. Nearly every knife recommended in these sets has been tested individually, so I feel confident saying you’ll be happily slicing, sawing, and coring with every recommended option.

Read on for our top knife set picks, including a couple of slightly more expansive options with a knife block and steak knives for those who want some extra pieces.

Latest in this upgrade: Editors spent some extended time with our top picks and we’ve added their long-term user notes.

Individual Mac knives have come out on top in our testing time and time again for their high-quality construction, ultrasharp blades, lightweight feel, and middle-of-the-road price point. This three-piece set is made up of a chef’s and petty knife that are the top overall picks in their respective categories, and a bread knife that’s essentially a luxe version of our favorite serrated knife.

Recent findings suggest that in testing, the Mac Professional Chef’s Knife was versatile and comfortable to use thanks to its ergonomic pakkawood handle, able to work through a giant mound of veggies efficiently without making our hands cramp up. Its blade was one of the sharpest we tested and combines the best qualities of Japanese- and Western-style chef’s knives in both its material and shape. Made of molybdenum high carbon steel, it strikes a balance between the brittle (but extra-sharp) steel used in Japanese blades and the softer, more durable steel typical of a Western knife. Similarly, its shape is a hybrid of the rounded edge of a Western-style blade and the straighter edge of a Japanese knife.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, we are also substantial fans of Mac’s Professional Series petty knife, and for similar reasons: It’s razor-sharp and offers a unique shape that splits the difference between a utility knife and paring knife.

The bread knife included in this set is also part of Mac’s Professional Series. It’s a tier up from the Superior Series knife that won our bread knife test, which is evident in its build quality: While it features the same scalloped blade of the Superior Series knife, it has a metal bolster that makes for a more seamless connection between the blade and handle, and a more balanced overall feel while slicing.

It has been revealed that in the long run: I used these Mac knives for more than a year (the chef’s knife I used for five) and they served me well the whole time. The paring knife is on the long side so it’s better suited to things like cutting hard cheeses than peeling or coring, though I prefer using a Y-peeler and an apple corer anyway. But because it’s longer, it was also easier to sharpen. The bread knife is perfect. The shape of the serrations and curve of the blade provide excellent leverage, and because they’re wavy instead of pointy, I didn’t notice loss of sharpness at all. It’s also heavy enough that its weight helps me push through without tearing.

Recent findings suggest that and then there is the chef’s knife. The old standby, loved by every reviewer and Test Kitchen editor who has tried it. The balance, weight, and shape made it versatile, and the steel sharpened fantastically. However, after a couple years, my Mac did chip. I was able to resharpen and salvage it, but I’m not the only one who ended up with a chipped blade. The Mac we kept in house for long term testing also chipped after a few years. As reviewer Jesse Raub has noted in a number of his knife pieces, Japanese knives like the Mac are made from harder steel, so they don’t dull easily but they do chip. Personally, I find it one of those trade-offs you have to make when you’re picking a knife, and there is much good about the Mac that I still happily endorse it.

—Noah Kaufman, senior reviews editor.

Classic Damascus 3 Piece Knife Set.

If you like the high-end look of beautiful Damascus steel and prefer a more rounded belly to your chef’s knife (better for rocking chops on the board), this set from Shun may be the one for you. Shun’s knives consistently perform well in our testing, and each of these knives has earned a spot as a top pick in its category. And by buying them as a set, you’ll save a modest amount of money off the total cost of the individual knives.

Recent findings suggest that one of the things that sets Shun’s Classic line apart is that it features the brand’s proprietary VG-MAX core, a high carbon steel with additional metals like chromium and molybdenum added in the mix to help with corrosion resistance and sharpness. In testing, we found this made for blades that cut effortlessly through anything we threw at them and retained their sharpness over time.

The rounded pakkawood handles of the Classic line knives made each of them extremely comfortable to hold, and because the handles maintain an even thickness throughout their length, they allow each user to find the grip and hand positioning that’s best for them.

Industry observers note that shun’s knives are routinely some of the sharpest in our testing, and we appreciate the more Western-leaning hybrid shape of their blades. It makes them great options for anyone who wants the versatility of a Western chef’s knife while looking for the precision edge of Japanese gyuto. While Shun’s bread knife is a little short for our tastes, it was also the sharpest and easily sliced through everything during its round of testing, earning it a top pick in that category.

According to recent reports, in the long run: I’ve had these Shun knives for a year now, and they’re my go-to set. The chef’s knife is incredibly comfortable to hold. A smooth notch where the blade meets the handle gives me a comfortable spot to pinch-grip, and the handle fits my small hands. The blade’s shape lets me glide and rock through tough ingredients. The paring knife is sharp and precise enough to hull strawberries but sturdy enough to cut into a thick wedge of Manchego. At nine inches, the bread knife handles most sourdough miches with ease, though I occasionally wish it were a little longer for really wide ones.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

Renaissance 5-Piece Knife Set With Magnetic Board.

Spending $400 on a knife set, like the Mac and Shun options above, is a substantial investment, even if you’re getting three high-quality blades. For a more budget-friendly alternative, we recommend this four-knife set (it gets called a five-piece set because the knife board counts as a piece) from Mercer Culinary’s Renaissance line. It’s a great cheap option for anyone who wants reliable knives without committing to a premium price point.

Mercer’s knives have consistently performed well in our testing, from the Renaissance line to the more affordable Genesis and Millennia collections. Their Millennia 10-inch Wavy Edge Bread Knife, priced under $16 when bought on its own, is even one of our top picks. In our tests, the Mercer chef’s, bread, and paring knives all delivered clean, consistent cuts and maintained their edges well after repeated use. While they didn’t outperform our favorite pricier knives, they came surprisingly close considering they were less than half the cost. Made from high carbon steel with full-tang construction and durable handles, the knives in this Renaissance set feel solid, well-balanced, and easy to control.

While we prefer the Japanese petty knife over a Western utility knife shape, there’s enough value in the core three knives of this set that we think it’s worth it for anyone who wants an affordable refresh or is stocking their kitchen for the first time.

In our testing for the best chef’s knives, Hedley & Bennett’s chef’s knife stood out as well-balanced, comfortable to grip, and easy to maneuver thanks to the seamless transition between the handle and blade. After months of use, our Test Kitchen editors were impressed with how well it held up. And while testers preferred the Mac, if you’re looking to bring some fun color into your kitchen while still investing in a high-performing knife set, Hedley & Bennett is a great choice.

In a recent development, this set includes a utility knife rather than a paring knife. It’s about two inches longer than a traditional paring knife (5.6 inches versus 3.5), making it a bit more versatile for larger tasks, such as slicing an oversized apple.

The bread knife is on the shorter side, at only 8.6 inches, but its sharp, tapered serrated edge allows for more controlled, precise cuts than some straight-blade designs. Deputy Food Editor Hana Asbrink notes that the blade’s slope also helps prevent your knuckles from hitting the cutting board, a common concern with bread knives that maintain the same width along the entire blade.

While they aren’t the sharpest knives out of the box, they’re made of high carbon stainless steel and can be easily sharpened to a finer edge. While we think most home cooks would like this set, its biggest advantage is the variety of colorways, which make for a more aesthetically pleasing kitchen.

According to recent reports, in the long run: I’m in a less-is-more phase of my life, mostly because my shoe box of a kitchen leaves little room for 10 knives. So the pared down three from Hedley & Bennett fits perfectly in my space. They’re lightweight and the tapered spines have contributed to a welcome feeling of precision when using them. The chef’s knife gets the most use—there’s something rhythmic about slicing garlic with it. But the utility knife has come in handy more often than I thought. I’ve used it, along with my trusty kitchen shears, to break down whole chickens. And the angled tip of the serrated knife has made it useful for more than sawing through crusty bread. The blade shape helps for more delicate work like piercing tomato skin without mangling it.

In a recent development, with use, a few minor scuffs and scratches have started to show. My colleagues have also warned me that the handles can crack over time, though that hasn’t been an glitch for me over the first several months. Bless the greater knife powers that be. I do make a point of never leaving my knives in the sink and always drying them thoroughly after washing.

—Nina Moskowitz, associate cooking editor.

Industry observers note that the Wüsthof Classic line helped define high-end knives both at home and in professional kitchens for decades. Over the years, Wüsthof Classic set the standard for what to expect for performance and durability—full-tang construction, high carbon stainless steel, and a razor-sharp edge that’s easy to maintain. In our tests, Wüsthof’s 8" chef’s knife has been a standout for many years, and the included bread knife and paring knife are also great options.

The significant catch is that many cooks prefer the more nimble Japanese-style and hybrid knives, and Wüsthof’s heritage puts its Classic line in a more expensive bracket. Still, if you prefer the heft and durability of Western-style knife set, it’s hard to go wrong with this one—and they’ll last a lifetime with good upkeep.

Classic Essential Knife Block, Set of 7.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a more expansive knife set beyond our essential three-piece recommendation, Shun’s Classic line stands out. This seven-piece set includes the core trio—a chef’s knife, paring knife, and bread knife—plus two smart additions: a 6-inch petty knife and a pair of herb shears. The petty knife fills that sweet spot between a paring and a chef’s knife, perfect for tasks that need more precision than a substantial blade allows but would overwhelm a smaller one, like slicing citrus or trimming proteins.

It has been revealed that the herb shears are a surprisingly handy upgrade. Instead of dragging out a cutting board just to mince some parsley or chives, you can snip them straight into a salad, soup, or garnish. Still, this is a good example of where a large set can sell you short: herb shears are less versatile than a standard set of heavy-duty kitchen shears.

The set also comes with a honing steel to keep your knives sharp and a sleek 11-slot bamboo storage block, which gives you extra space to add other styles down the line, like a nakiri for vegetable prep, a santoku, or even a cleaver.

Sources indicate that in the long run: By jumping up to the larger seven-piece set I got to add my favorite part of the set: the herb scissors. I use them to snip parsley right over a finished dish without pulling out a cutting board. They’re small, but they can still cut raw chicken into chunks when I don’t feel like reaching for a knife. Just be sure to hand-wash and towel-dry them right away. If you leave them dripping wet, they will get watermarks.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

Large knife sets that come with a storage block are handy—it’s literally a one-stop shop. And if you’re a fan of serving grilled ribeyes whole to your guests, you’re going to need some sharp steak knives. Global’s knives are strong performers in our tests, and their unibody construction makes them easy to clean and maintain. We also like their unique steel, which retains sharpness without being as brittle as other alloys.

According to recent reports, while they can be polarizing, many people find their dimpled steel handles comfortable to hold, and their knives come sharp out of the box. A massive reason we like this large set over other options is that larger knife sets are usually extremely expensive, or they’re made up of a knife maker's budget line. Here you see strong value for great knives, and the inclusion of a petty knife, a chef’s knife, and a kiritsuke-style slicing knife means there’s nothing you won’t be able to cut with swiftness and precision.

Given its size, it’s a well-balanced set, and the inclusion of the serrated utility knife is a nice touch for slicing tomatoes or peeling squash. It may feel like a hefty sticker price, but you’d be hard-pressed to find this many high-quality knives at this price point from other brands.

Recent findings suggest that in the long run: While the Shun knives are my home set, the Global Chef’s knife is the one I always use when I’m working in the Test Kitchen. The balance and the size of the knives in this set (a slightly shorter chef’s and bread knives) are perfect for smaller women. Other BA editors have echoed this idea in the past. The secret is in the handle. Its dimpled steel gives you a secure grip, and it starts wide before tapering in, which makes it perfect for small hands. It feels hefty (it’s full of sand) while still being lightweight, which matters when you need to stay nimble with your knife cuts.

—Olivia Tarantino, senior reviews editor.

Industry observers note that we’ve been testing knives for years now, and we have found that the same brands tend to come out on top across each knife category. Luckily for you, aspiring knife set purchasers, that means we’ve had no trouble finding three-piece sets from brands we know and love that feature product-test-winning, quality knives our team of experts can vouch for. Each set listed above is made up of individual knives we’ve tested against a long list of competitors and wholeheartedly approve of.

Head over to our individual reviews of the best chef’s knives, best bread knives, and best paring knives for even more information.

How many knives do you need in a knife set?

It has been revealed that we firmly believe that three knives are all you really need: a chef’s knife, a paring knife, and a bread knife. Together, they cover just about every essential kitchen task, from chopping vegetables to slicing crusty loaves.

That noted, if you’re looking to upgrade or expand your collection, three additional knives are excellent additions: a nakiri knife, a petty knife, and a cleaver. While not essential, they’re nice to have: the nakiri offers extra precision for vegetable prep, the petty knife is ideal for those in-between tasks that a paring or chef’s knife might not handle quite as neatly, and a cleaver can help tackle larger chopping tasks (or precision cuts with a Chinese cleaver).

Which is the best brand for knives?

Mac has come out on top of our knife testing across the three core knives—chef’s, serrated, and paring—but the question itself is sort of like asking “who is the best guitar player.” Different people will find different knife shapes, weights, and handle styles better or worse for their hands. And, there are a lot of small elite knife makers out there that make items that aren’t just kitchen tools, but works of art. If you want to investigate some of those, we’d encourage you to check out a shop like Chubo Knives for elite Japanese blades.

It has been revealed that but as far as affordable, widely available knives go, Mac’s routinely outperformed the competition. They are made in Japan from molybdenum high carbon steel, which blends the durability of Western-style steel with the precision sharpness of traditional Japanese blades. The result is a knife that’s lightweight, versatile, and sharp. Mac’s bread knife took the top spot in our testing thanks to its 10.5-inch blade, which is an inch and a half longer than most. That extra length makes it easier to slice through wide loaves like focaccia in a single stroke.

Are expensive knife sets worth it?

Industry observers note that we stand by all of our recommended knives, but what you will get if you buy higher-end knives are blades made from better steel that are finished with more care. That means they’ll hold an edge longer, require less sharpening, and last for years with proper care. For most home cooks, it’s worth investing at least $150–$200 in a chef’s knife since it’s the blade you’ll reach for every day. Secondary knives like paring, bread, or utility knives don’t need to be as pricey, but if you use them often, it may be worth upgrading those too (and getting them as part of a bundle in a small knife set is a good way to do that).

Read more here about how much you should spend on a knife.

Is it better to buy knives individually or as a set?

According to recent reports, it depends on your priorities. The great part about a knife set is that it’s a one-and-done purchase. You get the three essentials (chef’s, bread, and paring knives), and you can trust that each knife in the set has been tested to perform at a high level. That noted, buying individually gives you more flexibility. Maybe you prefer a 6-inch chef’s knife over an 8-inch or a longer bread knife like Mac’s 10.5-inch version over Shun’s 9-inch or Hedley & Bennett’s 8.6-inch tapered blade. Think of a set as a strong starting point: It gets you well-equipped right away, but you can always mix and match later as you learn what sizes and styles feel best in your hand.

Is it cheaper to buy knives in a set?

In general, yes—most manufacturers will offer at least some discount when you buy knives as a set rather than one at a time. How much of a discount? Well, that varies. For some brands, buying a three-piece set is like getting a third knife for free. For others, you might only save a few bucks. Still, many sets will also go on sale, adding even more savings to the already discounted knives. At the end of the day, it’s worth pricing out each knife in a set to see how much you’ll save by buying the bundle, and weigh that against being able to pick your favorite knife from each type. Still, we find that if you’re a fan of one knife from a brand, you’ll probably enjoy the handle style and comfort of other knives from the same brand—combined with some savings, you get a strong argument for picking out a knife set when you need a kitchen refresh.

What’s the best way to store your knives?

Proper storage is just as important as proper sharpening when it comes to keeping your knives in good shape. No knife should ever be tossed into a drawer with other utensils—that’s a quick way to dull the edge, damage the blade, or worse, hurt someone.

It has been revealed that the best storage option depends on your kitchen setup and preferences, but our favorite is a magnetic strip mounted on the wall. It keeps blades accessible, protects the edge, and works for all shapes and sizes, whether you’ve got a slim paring knife, a hefty cleaver, or even kitchen shears. Another major plus: magnetic strips take up zero counter or drawer space and are easy to clean with a quick wipe. These are our favorite magnetic strips.

Industry observers note that jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper.

Additional testing by Olivia Tarantino and Noah Kaufman.

It All Comes Together in Chattanooga

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that chattanooga has always been a city of convergence.
  • The destinations collected here allow for all sorts of gatherings: a railroad terminal built to serve historic crowds, now repurposed; a riverfront freighted with Cherokee history where folks now gather for performances; and even a whiskey company that rallied the community to change state law.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, chattanooga may be best known for its natural beauty, surrounded by mountains, valleys, and the Tennessee River. This charming Appalachian city is also home to annual music festivals like the IBMA World of Bluegrass and the 3 Sisters Bluegrass Festival. The streets and venues fill with musicians and fans dedicated to upholding the traditions of bluegrass music.

It has been revealed that chattanooga has always been a city of convergence. Long before trains arrived, the river drew people through a narrow passage in the mountains; later came traders, artists, and entrepreneurs. At festival time, bluegrass becomes the city’s soundtrack, with impromptu performances and jams ranging all across town. Many of the local hot spots are pressed into service as music venues.

The destinations collected here allow for all sorts of gatherings: a railroad terminal built to serve historic crowds, now repurposed; a riverfront freighted with Cherokee history where folks now gather for performances; and even a whiskey company that rallied the community to change state law. Taken as a whole, they reveal a city profoundly shaped around the possibilities of people coming together.

It has been revealed that begin at the building that made Chattanooga synonymous with arrival. Terminal Station opened in 1909 and at its peak handled nearly 50 trains a day, turning its grand waiting room into a literal crossroads of travelers, soldiers, workers, and families. Passenger service ended in 1970, but the station survived demolition and was reborn as the Chattanooga Choo Choo. Today the former terminal is once again centered around travel: the Hotel Chalet, restaurants, music venues, comedy, gardens, and Station Street all radiate from the old rail hub.

On Walden’s Ridge atop Signal Mountain, neighbors, musicians, and visitors have been uniting around music for years, sharing both a room and a repertoire. The original Mountain Opry began in 1979 and spent more than four decades presenting bluegrass and folk music at the Walden’s Ridge Civic Center before being reborn at the historic Bachman Community Center in 2021 as the Latest Mountain Opry. It lives on as a monthly tradition, with live bluegrass in the old school auditorium.

Follow the river west into the landscape that made Chattanooga a crossroads long before there was a city here. The Tennessee River Gorge runs for roughly 27 miles through the Cumberland Mountains, and archaeological evidence points to human presence here for at least 10,000 years. The river served as a travel corridor, and more recently communities, commerce, military movements, and industry have all depended on navigating through this narrow passage. Today the Tennessee River Gorge Trust protects more than 17,000 acres of the gorge and promotes hiking, paddling, camping, research, and education — turning an ancient corridor into a modern destination for conservation and outdoor life. Among other events, the gorge hosts Chattajack, a 31-mile paddleboard and kayak race. Visitors should also explore Williams Island, home to hundreds of acres of wilderness and only accessible by boat.

Ross’s Landing, along the riverfront, was associated with Cherokee businessman and later Principal Chief John Ross, serving as a ferry and trading location. In 1838, it also became a departure point during the forced removal of Cherokee people on the Trail of Tears. An art installation in the park commemorates their forcible departure. Today the riverfront is once again a major public space, with lawns, an amphitheater, a marina, promenades, and interpretive features hosting local events like Riverfront Nights free summer concert series and the Chattanooga River Games. Just upstream, the Walnut Street bridge reopened in October 2026, restoring one of downtown’s best-loved pedestrian connections across the Tennessee River after a major renovation.

Classic hospitality can be found here, at Chattanooga’s oldest hotel. The Read House traces its hotel history back roughly 150 years, while its present interiors lean into the glamour of the 1920s. Its most famous story belongs to Room 311: The room is mentioned to be haunted by the ghost of Annalisa Netherly, a guest from the 1920s. Tours keep the tale alive. The grand lobby and lively barroom conversation make this a hot spot for visitors to share their stories.

According to recent reports, at Chattanooga Whiskey, the convivial spirit turned into political action. When the tech giant was founded in 2011, state law still prevented distilling spirits in Hamilton County. Its founders launched the “Vote Whiskey” campaign, held public events, and pushed for a change in Tennessee law. The change passed into law in 2013, making legal distilling possible in the city again for the first time in more than a century. Production began at the Experimental Distillery in 2015, and regular tours are available, along with tastings of their signature Tennessee High Malt whiskey.

In a recent development, set above the Tennessee River in a historic downtown district, Bluff View brings together the River Gallery, sculpture garden, Bluff View Inn, Rembrandt’s Coffee House, Tony’s Pasta Shop, a bakery, patios, paths, and scenic overlooks. The appeal is less a single attraction than the way all of the pieces connect: art leads to coffee, coffee to a garden, and the garden to a view across the river.

In September 1863, Union and Confederate armies collided at Chickamauga in one of the Civil War’s bloodiest battles; the battlefield later became part of the nation’s first national military park. Over time, a second layer of communal memory accumulated here: ghost stories, especially the local legend of “Old Green Eyes.” There are many explanations for this mysterious apparition. One suggests it’s the spirit of a soldier. Another states the ghostly presence was there long before the Civil War. An annual October festival celebrates the legend. It’s just another example of how history and myth can exist in the same remarkable landscape.

In the early 1970s, less than 1% of U.S. households owned a home computer. (Today, the figure is closer to 98%.) But after Appleâs first Apple 1 computer arrived on the market in 1976, by the 1980s that figure had ballooned to almost one-fifth, showing that the computer age had well and truly begun.

Sources indicate that the original Apple 1, however, retailed at just over $660 (equivalent to almost $4,000 today), making it something of a status symbol among 1970s households. Nor was the at-home personal computer the only item that would have been considered something of a luxury back then that today we rather take for granted.

According to recent reports, by the end of the 1960s, barely 20% of U.S. households had made the switch to color television, but adoption was quick in the 1970s so that by the middle of the decade almost half of American homes had a color TV set. For a time, though, having access to color television wasnât quite as established a norm as it is today.

In a recent development, the first VCR systems were introduced in the 1950s, but were for a long time used almost exclusively among broadcast networks. It wasnât until the 1970s that commercial and domestic video cassette recorders became a household staple, with Sony introducing its U-matic system in 1971. It took several years for VCRs to become affordable for many U.S. households, however, making these early systems, in the formatâs early years, something of a rarity.

Sources indicate that in the 1960s and early â70s, video games were all but exclusively confined to gaming arcades, but the arrival of consoles like the Magnavox Odyssey (in 1972) and the Atari 2600 (in 1977) brought video games into American homes for the first time. At around $100 each, however (equivalent to more than eight times as much today), not everyone could afford an early game console, making early models like these a luxury for only higher-earning households. Today, youâll find a video game console in more than half of U.S. homes.

It has been revealed that touch-tone dialing was introduced in 1963, and gradually ousted the slower and more mechanical rotary dial phones as they became more popular. The takeover was a slow one, however (not least because touch-tone keypads were initially only available as a premium monthly service), making the newer models a luxury relatively few households could afford.

Recent findings suggest that as the early teenage rock and roll fans of the '50s and '60s grew up and settled down in the 1970s, they took their love of music with them, and by the end of the decade one-third of US homes had a hi-fi stereo system. Depending on quality and brand, however, such systems were often prohibitively costly and it wasnât until the '80sand '90s that home stereo systems became more popular than ever. Â.

The first automatic answering machine was developed way back in the 1930s, but domestic systems that allowed callers to record personal messages on a spool of reel-to-reel tape were first introduced in 1971. Early answering machines were bulky, slow, and remarkably costly, however, some early models retailed for upwards of $500 or more.

Although instant cameras had been on the market for more than 20 years by then, the arrival of Polaroidâs SX-70 instant camera in 1972 marked a new era in photography, with people waiting only a matter of minutes to develop their own pictures, without the need for a laboratory, for the first time. The SX-70 was an instant hit (ironically enough), but its high price pointâ$180 per unit, equivalent to more than $1,400 todayâmade it popular only with artists, professionals, and the ultra-wealthy.

Even the humble trash compactor was something of a luxury household appliance in the 1970s, with commercial models selling for more than $200 (equivalent to over five times that amount today).

According to recent reports, wood-paneled, carpeted wall-to-wall, and fitted out with beer pumps, cocktail-making kits, ice boxes, and wine racks, an at-home bar became a quintessential aspirational feature for many 1970s homeownersâbut fitting, running, and stocking one made them often impossibly expensive. Out of everywhere, they proved particularly popular in the Midwest, giving homeowners and their neighbors and friends somewhere cozy and social to hang out when the weather outside turned wintry.

According to recent reports, waterbeds proved all the rage in the late '60s and '70s, eventually becoming a $2 billion industry before the market popped (so to speak) in the later 20th century. Although associated with glamor and luxury in their heyday (Hugh Hefner famously had two at the Playboy Mansion), their cost and their maintenance made them squarely something only the most affluent could afford.

Sources indicate that âBlow dryersâthe handâheld, hotâair guns that have revolutionized hair stylingâare becoming essential grooming aids for both sexes and all ages,â reported the Newly introduced York Times in 1978. Although sales peaked at over 16 million in the mid 1970s, before then blow-dryers were something of a luxury, with the Times charting the deviceâs shift throughout the 1970s âfrom a luxury product for women to an essential grooming tool for all segments of the American population.â.

The KitchenAid brand debuted way back in the 1910s, with its mechanical food mixers first becoming commercially successful in the suburban homes of the â20s and '30s. Although a home bakerâs staple today, the brand has long been a luxury one, with early models costing the equivalent of several thousand dollars today. By the 1970s, an increasingly competitive market had brought the price down somewhat, but food mixers and other similar appliances were still something of a luxury for a home bakerâalthough the real flex was to have one that color-coordinated with the rest of your kitchen.

The first domestic microwave oven went on sale to the public back in 1955, priced at just shy of $1,300 (equivalent to an eye-watering $16,000 today). Even by two decades later, though, the microwave was still something of a premium appliance, retailing at up to $500 or more (which is still over $3,000 in 2020s terms).

Less than a fifth of US households had a dishwasher at the beginning of the 1970s. Although this was the decade that saw them become far more of a household staple than they ever had before, they remained an expensive luxury item for several years to come.

According to recent reports, census data indicated that four-fifths of American homes had a refrigerator by as far back as the 1950s, with one in eight having a second refrigerator by the end of the 1970s. Although many came with a built-in icebox, in which homeowners could store manual trays of ice cubes for ready use, through-the-door ice dispensers were still a luxury high-end feature, only available through premium brands. Countertop ice-makers, likewise, remained an appliance only the most affluent homeowners could splash out on.

According to recent reports, less than one in three American homes had air conditioning in the 1970s, and that number had barely increased by the end of the decade. Adoption of AC was decidedly regional (more southern houses had it installed than in New England, understandably), but as prices dropped and the technology became more widespread, even more houses gradually signed up.

The perfect accompaniment to your countertop ice-maker, electric ice-crushers were a surefire way of wowing your dinner party guests in the 1970s, but only to those who were able to afford them.

While above-ground pools became more affordable in the 1970s through improvements in manufacturing, construction of an in-ground pool was a prohibitively expensive luxury for many US households, with costs typically in excess of $3,000âequivalent to over $26,000 todayâfor even a small one.

By 1970, almost one-fifth of US houses still had no car at all, but just 29% were in a strong enough financial position to run two vehicles (a figure that has since increased by half).

Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1588 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that “Dinner is never just dinner.
  • I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes.
  • According to recent reports, bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that “Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”.

I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and host of the newly-introduced food show Salt The Water presented by Brami are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

According to recent reports, bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos. “I am a family-style cooker when I’m hosting, and I just want to fill people up. I want to fill their glasses up; I want to fill their plates up. And the best compliment that I could ever get is having to tell someone, ‘Hey man, it’s really time to go home because I am exhausted and I need to go to bed.’”.

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

It has been revealed that “On a table, I will always have one kind of grand slam major, big dish, and then there’s all the supporting actors on the table,” Bruno says. While she uses saved folders on Instagram and Pinterest and likes to browse the Bon Appétit app, Bruno primarily looks to the market for inspiration, describing herself as a “very, very in-season cooker.” “I have so many recipes saved, and sometimes some of those get used, but there is something that just happens when you’re walking, and you see all of these fresh ingredients, and you just get to create a dish right in front of you.”.

Industry observers note that bruno’s main tip for anxious hosts is to prep as much in advance as possible. “Sauces and dressings you can absolutely do the day before, and that alleviates so much time the day of. You could go as far as literally setting your entire table the way you want it to be set with napkins, plates, silverware,” Bruno says.

It has been revealed that “Lighting is a huge thing,” Bruno claims. For evening soirees, she kisses the big overhead light goodbye, opting instead for lower light from lamps and candles tucked into corners to make the space feel moody. “The mood needs to be right, and you want to feel sexy when you walk into somebody’s home,” she says.

Bruno worked in restaurants and went to culinary school in Paris, where she learned the importance of maintaining a clean workspace. “If something spills right then and there, you are wiping it right then and there. If you use the spoon and you’re done, it’s going in the dishwasher. Cleaning as you go is a big step,” she notes.

It has been revealed that when hosting a more intimate event, one of Bruno’s favorite moves takes the form of an interactive game meant to encourage a bit of deep conversation. “Right before I serve dessert, I have everyone lift up their plate, and there is a little note underneath,” she claims. The note has a question on it, either handwritten or printed depending on how much time Bruno has, and every question is different. “It adds a layer of, ‘Oh, our conversation maybe wouldn’t have gone here…. I just love getting to more juicy parts of the person, whether it’s a close friend or an absolute stranger, and it keeps people on their toes,” she says.

Sources indicate that “It’s so easy to stay in host mode and think that you have to do all of these things to please people. But as soon as people arrive, it’s almost like, your job is done—or at least as soon as you drop the food, your job is done. And now you get to sit back and enjoy what you’ve done and be a part of it, because the worst feeling ever is you had all these people over, whether it’s four people or 10 people, and you were stuck in the kitchen and no one got to see you. So be a guest,” Bruno says.

Sources indicate that bruno recounts a recent conversation with a friend who was afraid, on the one hand, to try making and serving something newly introduced, but felt the dishes that were in her repertoire were too simple for tech giant. “You should never apologize for something that you’re cooking. If you are putting yourself out there and you want to cook something out of your realm, and, say it absolutely f*#%ing fails, that’s fine. I feel like your guests are going to be like, ‘Awesome. We will take a bite and not tell you our honest answer, and then we’re going to order a pizza, and it’s going to be amazing.’ The triumph of just trying is so much bigger than the actual meal,” Bruno says. “Food is the second tier. It’s more about the people around your table. You could serve potato chips and dip and people will actually be pretty happy,” she adds.

In a recent development, “Nine out of 10 times, if I am cooking for people, there is going to be a pasta dish on the table,” Bruno claims. She’s a big fan of the protein pasta brand Brami, and not just because she just partnered with them on a YouTube show—she says the brand has organically become the only pasta she keeps at home.

Sources indicate that as for sauce, Bruno’s go-to is a spicy vodka. “If I’m making it at home, I’m actually leaving out the vodka and I’m swapping in mezcal, and it gives such a sneaky, smoky flavor that everyone will ask [about it]. And I will then go even further and usually pair it with a mezcal cocktail,” she claims.

Now that you know all of Bruno’s tips, these are the products she uses to make gatherings more special and less stressful.

Bruno always keeps three types of olive oil on hand: “One that is not so fancy and you could fry or make dressing with it—just one that’s kind of the back burner; a topping oil; and then an amazing peppery oil that you would maybe more so dip bread in or drizzle on top.”.

Industry observers note that “Flaky salt is always in my house,” Bruno claims. She typically opts for either Maldon or a fleur de sel.

According to recent reports, “We could consider Brami a staple. I mean, [my husband and I] cook it at least two times a week, whether there’s meat thrown in it or it’s just a sauce or a pesto or it's anything in between,” Bruno says.

Bird’s Eye Maple Wood Chopping Board.

Palio Round Serving Platter The Giraffe.

It has been revealed that for hosting, I love massive platters. Whether they’re vintage or latest, I kind of love mixing those two together on the table,” Bruno says. She likes having a collection of larger serveware specifically for hosting: “It’s kind of like your special stuff that you take out for friends.”.

1960s French Chrome Swan Handle Tray.

Jean Couzon Silverplate Serving Tray Fish Handles.

1970's Kromex Sculptura Walnut Accent Lazy Susan Serving Tray.

Antique Silver Plated Large Oval Tray.

Large Footed Silver Plated Butler’s Tray With Ornate Handles and Feet Bar Drinks Serving.

“I love silver, so I have a lot of silver trays, a lot of silver bowls. I think it makes a table,” Bruno claims. “I have quite the collection. I almost always buy vintage or second-hand when it comes to silver. There’s simply something about the life the piece had,” she adds.

Sources indicate that “I recently splurged and got a really lovely cream and red dishware set from Porta. That was a big purchase for me, and it is a purchase that I am excited to bring out sparingly because I don’t want anything to break,” Bruno indicates.

When it comes to flatware, Bruno is a Sabre person. “I have three different colors in my house. It’s the only cutlery that I have at this point,” she indicates.

Sources indicate that “We are a big wine-drinking family, so I have a wine fridge. There are on average at least 15 bottles of wine in that fridge always, and it is a variety because you never know what somebody likes,” Bruno says.

In a recent development, when hosting, Bruno keeps a candle burning in her bathroom and on the kitchen counter at all times. She’s partial to Keap’s Wood Cabin scent, which she orders in bulk for both her own home and her event space, Frank’s House.

In a recent development, vintage St. James Silver Ice Bucket.

Stainless Steel Ice Bucket with Wood Accents.

1960s Swedish Cultura Stainless Steel Ice Bucket.

French Linen Tablecloth in Gingham.

Industry observers note that bruno loves a swanky ice bucket to keep bottles chilled in style, and she turns to tablecloths when she needs a pop of color. As for candlesticks, she likes the two-tone Dryp candles from Ferm Living.
