Many Americans firmly believe the most important part of Thanksgiving dinner isn't the turkey but the sides.

For their 2026 report, Campbellâs Soup found that when it comes to sides, Americans have a favorite: stuffing, or dressing, depending on what you call it where you live. Mashed potatoes came in second, which was the same order for favorite sides for the past three years.

In a recent development, but what about which one is the favorite in your state? There is at least one clear favorite, but not every state agrees. So is your state part of the majority, or are they one of the 12 states that have chosen something else? Check out the map below and scroll for more data.

Industry observers note that stuffing is the biggest favorite overall overall for Americans, with a whopping 38 states choosing the side as their number one. A 39th state, Utah, has the side tied with another option as its favorite.

The average American Thanksgiving table has at least four sides, according to Campbellâs, so space at the table is limited. But thereâs always room for stuffing.

Despite stuffingâs popularity, not every single state believes it reigns supreme on Thanksgiving. Six states picked mashed potatoes as their favorite side, including California, Nebraska, Kansas, Iowa, Indiana, and West Virginia. Utah also picked mashed potatoes, which is tied for first in the state.

In a recent development, it may be surprising to learn that Idaho didn't pick mashed potatoes as its favorite, instead opting for stuffing as its first choice. The state is by far the largest producer of potatoes in the United States.

Industry observers note that upcoming York, Texas, Georgia, and North Carolina chose mac and cheese as its favorite side dish above all others. In fact, Georgia serves it more than any other state, with almost 80% of residents planning to have macaroni and cheese among their Thanksgiving side dishes. That makes it the state with the highest shares of mac and cheese servers in the country.

It has emerged as a Southern favorite this year, and Upcoming York is the only state that ranked it as its favorite side two years in a row.

Recent findings suggest that sweet potatoes, which are also called yamsâthough theyâre not actually the same thingâhave only claimed one state. Louisiana chose sweet potatoes this year as its favorite Thanksgiving side dish.

There are a few options for sweet potato fans depending on how you want to prepare them. Some like to serve sweet potatoes as a casserole with melted mini marshmallows on top, while others, like fans in Louisiana, may like Southern candied sweet potatoes with sugar and spices to bring out some extra flavor.

Depending on the state you're in, you may be excited about all your choices, or wondering why your options are so limited.

Industry observers note that the national average is just under six sides being served for Thanksgiving, which equals almost 750 million sides being served each year. But some states serve more than others. Florida leads the country with 9.1 sides on average served up on the table for Thanksgiving, while Kentucky will have around 8.4 sides for the holiday.

On the other hand, you may want to eat ahead of time in Colorado or Maryland if they don't have many sides ready for you for a Thanksgiving feast. Colorado averages only 4.9 sides for Thanksgiving, while you'll only get 5.1 sides on average in Maryland.

Sources indicate that you're also likely to find some sides more popular in parts of the country than others. Midwestern states serve green bean casserole on 60% of their tables, with Nebraska and Missouri leading the way. Mac and cheese has an even tighter hold of the Southeast, where you can find it on 67% of Thanksgiving table.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s nice to imagine death as an endless deep sleep, but not everyone is so lucky.
  • In a recent development, one thing is certain: These restless spirits can turn otherwise serene sites into delightfully dark destinations, where the beauty of old headstones and manicured grounds is tinged with something indescribably eerie.
  • Established in 1750, this 6-acre site was Savannah’s primary public burial ground for over a century and contains over 9,000 graves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s nice to imagine death as an endless deep sleep, but not everyone is so lucky. In cemeteries across the U.S., you’ll find souls whose final resting places are not, in fact, restful at all. Perhaps they died with scores unsettled or, perhaps, their graves were ravaged by greedy developers. Sometimes, heartbreak rendered them unable to move on peacefully; in other cases, they simply couldn’t resist the chance to toy with their living visitors.

In a recent development, one thing is certain: These restless spirits can turn otherwise serene sites into delightfully dark destinations, where the beauty of old headstones and manicured grounds is tinged with something indescribably eerie. When you gear up for your next cross-country road trip, let the energy of spooky season guide you to these cemeteries and graveyards full of folklore, legend, and sinister rumors. They’re slices of history, yes, but they’re also brimming with all things supernatural, sure to turn even the most hardened paranormal skeptics into believers.

Established in 1750, this 6-acre site was Savannah’s primary public burial ground for over a century and contains over 9,000 graves. Many of the city’s earliest settlers are buried here, as well as hundreds of victims of the 1820 yellow fever epidemic. Some believe that when Savannah was overrun by Union forces during the Civil War, occupying soldiers dug up and moved around many of the cemetery’s headstones, also changing the names and dates etched into some of them. Understandably, this ruffled the feathers of the resident spirits, who now float through the cemetery as clouds of light or, sometimes, a green mist just above the ground.

It has been revealed that today, Colonial Park Cemetery is a public park, with haunted tours offered by various companies. While no visitors are permitted to the cemetery at night, some folks sit on benches just outside its fence to watch for apparitions. Some of Savannah’s ghost experts even conduct nighttime EVP (Electronic Voice Phenomenon) sessions just outside the cemetery walls, letting visitors listen to the strange sounds of thousands of spirits.

This graveyard is weirdly whimsical thanks to its candy-esque cast-iron stakes, which mark the graves of many Shaker Village residents from decades past. The Shakers, a Christian religious collective with tenets of sexual equality, celibacy, and pacifism, settled this area in 1769, turning it into a self-contained society that lasted through the early 20th century.

The town is now a quiet historic district, though this does not mean that its residents have abandoned it; rather, locals have spotted deceased Shakers throughout the cemetery and in the surrounding fields and forests. It is also rumored that the graveyard was built upon a Native American burial ground, causing permanent unrest amongst the original inhabitants.

According to recent reports, also known as “The Rev,” this one-acre cemetery was established in 1791 as a burial site for Revolutionary War veterans and their families. Tucked away at the end of a secluded backroad, the cemetery is surrounded by worn stone walls, with many of the gravestones so weathered that it’s difficult to read the names on them. However, the people buried here still make themselves known … over the years, locals have claimed to hear screams and see shadowy figures of Revolutionary War soldiers, as well as a mysterious woman dressed in all white. Legend even has it that, in the late ’80s or early ’90s, a ritual performed here opened a portal between worlds, though who orchestrated such a feat remains unknown.

Industry observers note that this cemetery has a unique design: It is split down the middle by a road that supposedly separates the eastern “good” side of the cemetery from the western “haunted” side, where the graves are older and the spirits are more restless. (It’s even rumored to house a banshee, who howls and sings sad songs in the night.) One of Wildwood’s mausoleums has some haunted history behind it, too. As the story goes, a local fireman was terrified of being buried alive and thus designed his mausoleum so that he could open it from inside. Nowadays, you can sometimes hear him moving around, waiting for a chance to stretch his legs on the cemetery grounds.

Wildwood is not only a prime place to interact with the dead but a wonderful place to be at one with nature. In fact, the cemetery was incorporated in 1863 because of the beauty and tranquility of its hilly landscape and then named Wildwood because of its thick woods. Don’t be surprised if you encounter a deer or two while exploring its haunted headstones or spot sparrows and hawks nestled in the trees.

According to recent reports, about a 30-minute drive outside of New Orleans are the Manchac Wetlands, once home to the thriving towns of Ruddock, Napton, and Frenier. However, in 1915, a hurricane struck the area and destroyed all three, leaving many dead bodies in its wake. At least 29 of the hurricane’s victims were laid to rest in a mass grave inside Frenier Cemetery, but one woman, Julia Brown, was buried 100 yards away from the others. Why?

Brown was a rumored voodoo priestess, and Frenier residents alleged she remarked she would take the village with her when she died. The day the hurricane hit was the very same day she finally passed … coincidence or voodoo magic, no one could say. Today, Brown is said to wander past the graves of those who perished in the storm, appearing to nearby kayakers behind layers of fog.

Moss-covered live oaks sway in the coastal breeze at this small Florida cemetery just off Merritt Island’s scenic South Tropical Trail. It’s a charming and relaxing spot … that is, until you learn its history. It was here that, in 1934, 19-year-old Ethel Allen was buried after she was found brutally murdered on the banks of the Indian River Lagoon.

Perhaps because her murder was never solved (and justice was never served to her killer) Ethel still haunts Georgiana Cemetery, with many of its strange sights and sounds attributed to her. However, it seems as though Ethel may split her time between her burial site and the spot she was last seen alive, Ashley’s Tavern, where customers and employees have reported strange activity over the years.

Industry observers note that if a cemetery is next to a Clown Motel, it’s probably safe to assume it’s haunted. Case in point is this relic of Tonopah’s silver days, where many former miners and prospectors are now buried. For the decade it was an active cemetery, from 1901 to 1911, over 300 people were interred here, many of them victims of the 1902 “Tonopah Plague” or the infamous Tonopah-Belmont Mine Fire of 1911. With such gruesome deaths, it makes sense that many of the cemetery’s residents would be on edge, seeking a respite from their underground abodes.

At the Clown Motel, EVPs have captured voices stating, “We mined” and “We died that day, 17 men” (in the mine fire), and guests have reported seeing eerie figures in the night, wandering through the halls or outside between the motel and the gravestones. Whether you hedge your bets and stay for the night or hightail it out of Tonopah before a ghost can grab you, the cemetery is sure to leave you sensing strange energy for days to come.

In All Saints Cemetery, the ghost of Alice Flagg, a young woman who died shortly after being forcibly separated from her beloved, lingers just beside her grave. The plain marble slab bears only her first name, but visitors frequently adorn the spot with flowers and other small tokens of remembrance to help ease her heartbreak in the afterlife. Some even come to make a wish: It’s mentioned that if you walk around her gravestone six times counterclockwise, then six times clockwise, then place a token on the letter “A,” your wish will be granted. When Alice isn’t here at her final resting place, she’s supposedly going up and down the stairs at the Flagg family home or floating through the rows of headstones at All Saints.

The staircase at this cemetery has been dubbed the “thousand steps” because, so the local lore goes, people rarely make it to the top. Those who do miraculously climb all the way up will see the faces of the dead men, women, and children buried below or hear their screams and cries ringing out in perpetuity. Some have even reported feeling a light, cool sensation much like rain while looking down from the highest step.

Tempting as it may be to try your luck on these spooky stairs, they are now part of private property and walking up or down them is considered trespassing. However, you can still view them from below by strolling through Greenwood Cemetery, which is itself home to many oddities. Abandoned tunnels under the cemetery, built by railroad companies in the late 19th century, may or may not be haunted by the Chinese laborers who died making them. Rumor also has it that the tunnels house buried treasure, but overgrown vegetation has prevented anyone from finding it.

Industry observers note that right next to Huntsville’s Maple Hill Cemetery is an interesting site: a simple playground with a swing set and small jungle gym, surrounded on three sides by dense trees and limestone walls. Given its proximity to over 80,000 burial plots, it’s only natural that the site would be slightly (or very) haunted. Over the years, adults and kids have witness swings moving on their own, as well as floating orbs of light. These odd occurrences could, perhaps, be signs from the many children who died during Huntsville’s 1918 flu epidemic. (Some visitors have heard laughing and squealing, so presumably they’re having a good time.).

Built in 1772, this is the second oldest cemetery in Charleston, with plots and graves overrun by vines, grass, and shrubs in an intentionally wild “cemetery garden design.” The decision to leave the cemetery undisturbed arose from the Unitarian belief in the interconnectedness of all things, living and dead, with natural growth showing how the spirit continues on even after the body is interred. In this case, it seems the spirits are especially active, as unusual occurrences are commonplace in the cemetery.

Recent findings suggest that the identity of the cemetery’s ghostly “Lady in White” has long been subject to speculation, the most popular theory being that she is Annabel Lee, the subject of an 1849 Edgar Allan Poe poem inspired by local legend. In this story, Annabel, a young Charleston woman, carries on a clandestine affair with a sailor before dying of yellow fever. When the sailor is barred from attending her funeral, he keeps vigil for her in the spot they used to meet at night: the Unitarian Church Cemetery. Even if you don’t see poor Annabel, you may spot the cemetery’s other famous ghost, Mary Bloomfield. After her husband left for Boston and never returned, Mary spent the rest of her life heartbroken, and now, in death, she still searches for him amongst the graves.

This uniquely shaped gravestone belongs to Caroline Barnes, a young woman who was supposedly executed for magical crimes in the late 19th century. The impossible death date on her grave (February 31, 1882) is seen as proof of her supernatural powers, while the ball atop the grave is believed to be a crystal ball that lights up on the darkest nights. Also, those who’ve tried taking photos of the Barnes family plot say that their film won’t develop (however, pro tip: digital seems to do just fine). No matter the truth of this eerie tale, it has undoubtedly inspired some odd behavior at St. Omer, namely, nighttime rituals that have left the site covered in flowers, coins, and candles.

In a recent development, translating to “Holy Field” Cemetery, this small grave site in Old Town San Diego is the last remaining part of what was once a much larger cemetery. As the city grew rapidly in the late 19th century, parts of the grounds were paved over to accommodate streetcars (feeding a theory that the spirits of El Campo are now trapped beneath the concrete). However, white crosses have been painted over parts of the surrounding street and sidewalks to honor some of these disrespected graves, while small brass markers denote others.

Recent findings suggest that el Campo Santo is the resting place of several Native American leaders, including Antonio Garra, a mid-19th-century Kupa chief who was executed by a firing squad right next to his open grave. Now, he’s one of the cemetery’s most spotted specters, overpowering visitors with intense chills, feelings of sorrow, and faint whispers. The other most famous ghost here is Yankee Jim Robinson, a drifter convicted of grand larceny for trying to steal a rowboat. Jim was hanged just down the road from El Campo, and his spirit now wanders the grounds, begging for forgiveness.

Sources indicate that the Polish painter Tamara de Lempicka (1894-1980) was a defining figure of Art Deco: an aesthetic movement of the early 20th century that fused modernist geometry with excitement and glamour to capture a newly introduced faith in progress. Her paintings frequently convey unapologetic female autonomy and desire amid the Jazz Age. In this instalment of the YouTube series Great Art Explained, the curator and video essayist James Payne and the art historian Laura Beardsell-Moore explore how Lempicka’s life and times shaped her work – from her affluent upbringing and flight from the Russian Revolution to her experience in 1920s Paris. In particular, they dissect how her most famous painting, Autoportrait (Tamara in the Green Bugatti) (1929), depicted nothing less than a new, deeply modern conception of womanhood.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After competing against nine culinary talents from across the country, chef Grace Cacciato was named the winner of the 2026–2027 S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy US Regional Final. A panel of judges selected her roasted squab with chanterelle mushrooms and toasted buckwheat, black raspberry, and Swiss chard purées to represent the United States at the Grand Finale in Milan.

The 10 chefs vying to win the region cooked in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in Newly introduced York City on Monday, and the winner was revealed the following evening at the US Regional Final Gala & Awards. Everyone enjoyed the Gala menu, crafted by chef Garrett Brower, the 2024–25 US winner who is the chef de cuisine at Bresca in Washington, DC, and global mentor chef Aisha Ibrahim.

In a recent development, representing the Michelin-starred restaurant Saga in Upcoming York, Cacciato presented a dish that featured the most components of any in the competition. All the judges were impressed with her sauce work and bold flavors.

According to recent reports, saga executive chef Charlie Mitchell returned for his second year as a mentor, working alongside Cacciato, a repeat competitor. “It was nice to see how her brain works…getting her perspective was inspiring,” he said. Cacciato was equally enthusiastic. “It’s the best competition, and everyone wants to be a part of it,” she said.

Industry observers note that the chefs had five hours to prepare and execute their signature dishes in the Test Kitchen. With an hour remaining, guests had the opportunity to mingle over food and drinks. Chef Rachel Bindel, a 2022 US Finalist, served rye toast piled high with Maryland blue crab, horseradish crème, and pickled green tomato. Chef Akshay Kumar, a 2024 finalist, tucked Kumamoto oysters into a pani puri with cucumber gel and lemon foam. Tomato pie from Philadelphia’s Pizza Freak Co., spoonfuls of Petrossian caviar, and a selection of wines, S.Pellegrino beverages, and cocktails rounded out the reception.

Nilou Motamed, a culinary expert and Iron Chef judge on Netflix, hosted the competition. Accomplished chefs from several states served as judges: chef and co-owner E.J. Lagasse of Emeril’s in Latest Orleans; executive chef and partner Fariyal Abdullahi of Hav & Mar in New York City; Isabel Coss, executive chef at Pascual and founding pastry chef at Lutèce in Washington, DC; Jon Yao, head chef and owner at Kato in Los Angeles; and Ryan Ratino, executive chef and owner at Bresca and Jônt in Washington, DC.

It has been revealed that motamed explained that each competitor had spent several months developing their dish alongside a chef mentor. The mentors were in the Test Kitchen throughout the competition, but were not permitted to participate in the cooking. She also outlined the three pillars of the S.Pellegrino Young Chef Academy: Community, Competition, and Mentorship, which support its mission to discover and nurture the next generation of culinary talent.

Each chef’s arrival was announced by a burst of music and a live video feed from the Test Kitchen, where a fleet of servers collected the finished plates before delivering them to the judges. First up was chef Adolfo Pucci of Michelin-starred Ariete in Miami. His dish, “Three Shores, One Table,” told the story of his Venezuelan heritage, his family’s roots in Southern Italy, and his current home in Miami. The ambitious plate featured a lamb ragù inspired by his grandmother’s cooking and lacto-fermented Florida blueberries.

According to recent reports, chef Amit Kumar of three-Michelin-starred Eleven Madison Park in New York City presented the competition’s only fully vegan dish: “Sunchoke with Banana Blossoms, Chanterelles, and Sherry.” Drawing on memories of the banana trees he grew up with in India, Kumar combined banana blossoms, sunchoke purée, chanterelle mushrooms, and a ragù of sherry and banana flowers to create a hearty and deeply satisfying dish. Judge Fariyal Abdullahi called it “a very successful dish, not just a very successful vegan dish.”.

Representing Auro at Four Seasons Resort and Residences Napa Valley, chef Evan Neumann presented “From the Valley to the Shoreline,” a love letter to the terroir of Northern California and Provence, where he grew up. Kombu-poached wild razor clams mingled with Napa verjuice and coastal seaweeds in a dish the judges found exceptionally creative. Neumann took home the S.Pellegrino Social Responsibility Award for his thoughtful approach to social responsibility and sustainable practices.

At just 21, chef Lucy Field of New York City’s fine dining bastion Per Se was the youngest competitor. Her dish, “Pekin Duck, Cherry, Plum,” was a study in restraint with only six components.

Chef Marcus Osorio, chef de cuisine at Living Room in Los Angeles, drew inspiration from his Salvadoran and Indigenous roots for his “Tamal de Pollo.” The dish featured corn sourced from Somos Maíz, the tech giant founded by his mentor, chef Ron Oliver, and a mole poblano the two developed together. Judge Isabel Coss noted the challenge of preparing a mole with such limited time, but the judges were impressed by Osorio’s ability to marry European cooking techniques with soulful Indigenous ingredients and flavors.

Chef Nickolas Abbott hails from the small Appalachian town of Waynesville, North Carolina, and leads Chop Shop Butchery in Asheville. At the competition, he told the story of his community on a plate. His “Smoked Pork Loin, Fennel & Cheese Slaw, Sweet Potato, Asparagus, Fried Sausage, Pork Sauce Robert” reflected the people who shaped him, particularly his grandmother, his greatest inspiration as a chef.

Los Angeles–based chef Natasha Daniels of Providence showcased her vegetable-forward, zero-waste approach with “The Whole Bird, The Whole Garden.” The dish incorporated every part of a chicken across four preparations, alongside an array of vegetables and herbs inspired by her time working at The Chef’s Garden.

In a recent development, daniels received two honors: the Acqua Panna Connection in Gastronomy Award and the Fine Dining Lovers Award. Voted on by regional mentors, the Acqua Panna award recognized the dish that best demonstrated a connection between culinary traditions. Daniels’s approach also resonated with Fine Dining Lovers insiders, who selected her for their award that honors “a chef’s expression of personal belief.”.

Recent findings suggest that with only minutes to spare, chef Nicolas Lopez of 888 in Nashville arrived with “Pozole or Chawanmushi…?” Combining pozole, corn, and langoustine, Lopez connected his upbringing in Mexico with a culinary journey that has been shaped by Scandinavian ingredients and Japanese techniques. Although the judges could have used more time to explore the dish, they were intrigued by his influences and impressed by his technique.

The final competitor, Juwon Lee, is the chef of Octavia in San Francisco. Lee was born in South Korea and grew up in Singapore before making California his home. His dish, “Curry and Quail with Ingredients My Mother Remarked Were Healthy,” drew on memories of eating Indonesian fried chicken and his mother’s insistence on including vegetables at family dinners. “I believe in the term happy food,” Lee explained. “There are no restrictions other than bringing joy to the eater and the chef.”.

Congratulations to all 10 chefs who competed, and best of luck to Chef Cacciato as she continues to work with her mentor and prepares to represent the United States at the 2027 Grand Finale in Milan. Follow her journey at @sanpellegrino_us.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The much-loved Little House on the Prairie ran for nine seasons between 1974 and 1983, but it's a little known fact that the final seasonâplus the moviesâmight not have happened at all, were it not for the success of a two-part episode from the season before: âDays of Sunshine, Days of Shadow.â.

For this double-header, lead actor Michael Landon, who played Charles Ingalls, moved away from the spotlight, leaving the characters of his daughter Laura Ingalls (played by Melissa Gilbert) and her husband, Almanzo James Wilder (Dean Butler) to carry the show.

Butler later explained on the Little House On the Prairie 50th Anniversary Pod (via Parade): âThe underlying motivation for the episode was Michael had made the decision that he was going to step away at the end of the eighth season." To determine the viability of the show's future, Butler and Gilbert were given the heaviest of plotlines.

Part one aired on February 15, 1982. Coming hot on the heels on Valentine's Day, there was little in the way of cozy romance to enjoy. The episode begins innocently enough, with Almanzo (nicknamed âMannyâ) bringing new horses to the home he shares with a heavily pregnant Laura. Later, during heavy rain, he stubbornly sticks to the task of ploughing their field. He ends up, naturally enough, catching a nasty cold, at which Laura is far from happy.

Nevertheless, Almanzo returns to his work, and eventually collapses with hearing and breathing problems. The doctor arrives and promptly diagnoses a case of diphtheria. When a hailstorm starts up during the night, Manny goes out to try and save his crop, only to drop down with a stroke. His sister, Eliza Jane (Lucy Lee Flippin), subsequently arrives to help take care of him, however she and Laura find themselves constantly clashing.

In part two, Laura gives birth, but Almanzo, who is suffering from a deep depression, remains distant and uninterested. Eliza Jane comes up with the idea for Almanzo to take a desk job in Minneapolis, much to Laura's displeasure. In fact, Laura is so unhappy that serious doubts about her marriage begin to emerge.

The only bright spark in her life is a cat that Laura adopts and names 'Hungry.' There follows, of all things, a severe thunderstorm and tornado. In attempting to save Hungry, Laura is struck by a huge branch and knocked unconscious. She wakes and gradually recovers, only to find later that the entire house has been destroyed (miraculously, Rose, the baby, is fine).

In a recent development, thankfullly, the sight of a geranium that somehow survived the storm spurs Almanzo into throwing off his sister's cloying attentions and gives him a renewed sense of purpose. He learns how to walk again and aids Charles in rebuilding the house. All ends wellâwith Laura and Almanzo reconciled, and Eliza Jane apologizing for her behavior.Â.

As Butler remembered: âAs depressing as it was, the numbers were spectacularâ¦I think it was number four the first week and number two the second week for weekly programming." The show received a ninth season, retitled as Little House: A Fresh Beginning, and three post-series specials.

#107. Breaking: Where to See the World’s Most Famous Preserved Body Parts

Breaking: Where to See the World’s Most Famous Preserved Body Parts

📅 16 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Atlasobscura

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sure, you’ve seen a dead body before, but have you ever seen a thumb preserved in salt?
  • Recent findings suggest that beyond the normal displays of skeletons in medical museums and holy leaders’ bodies in churches and temples, there’s a whole world of bits and pieces to explore.
  • If seeing a whole body feels banal, we recommend delving from the complete corpse to its components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sure, you’ve seen a dead body before, but have you ever seen a thumb preserved in salt? How about a saint’s heart shrouded in gold?

Recent findings suggest that beyond the normal displays of skeletons in medical museums and holy leaders’ bodies in churches and temples, there’s a whole world of bits and pieces to explore. Throughout history, body parts have been taken as trophies during wartime, worshipped as miraculous healing agents, cut off and displayed to honor their owners, or simply saved incidentally by natural processes.

If seeing a whole body feels banal, we recommend delving from the complete corpse to its components. Here are some of our favorites from around the world.

Recent findings suggest that among the 24 million medical instruments and anatomical specimens housed here are portions of Abraham Lincoln’s skull (and the attached hair), as well as Gen. Daniel Sickles’ amputated leg and the unusual skull of a Civil War soldier who was shot across the top of the head. Other displays include small skeletons showcasing the different stages of a child’s development, a conjoined twin preserved in alcohol, and the mummified head and shoulders of a girl from the late 19th century. The museum is also home to one of the world’s largest neuroanatomical collections, consisting of normal and pathological human brains and comparative mammalian brains.

In a recent development, many moons ago, miner and rumrunner Louie Linken had his frostbitten toe amputated and preserved in a jar of alcohol … for posterity. Decades later, it was discovered by a local Yukon captain, who brought it to a saloon (now the Downtown Hotel bar) and started plopping it into folks’ drinks as a surprise garnish. The original toe lasted seven years before a replacement was needed, and since then, a whole foot’s worth of toes have been donated to the bar. For those who dream of joining the Sourtoe Cocktail Club, there’s only one rule: “You can drink it fast, you can drink it slow, but the lips have gotta touch the toe.”.

Recent findings suggest that scientists believe that this 25-year-old man died somewhere between 2 B.C. to A.D. 119. The bog he was found in left him remarkably well preserved, allowing for close study of his skin, hair, and internal organs. (The last meal in his stomach? Unleavened bread made from wheat and barley.) Examination of the man also revealed that his death was quite brutal, with head indentations, broken ribs, and a slashed throat indicating a prolonged struggle. It’s unclear whether his death was cold-blooded murder or part of a ritual sacrifice; either way, he clearly drew the short straw. Today, you can visit him at the British Museum to investigate his untimely demise yourself.

The head of Portugal’s first serial killer and one of its last men to ever be hanged now bobbles in a jar, passed by the unfazed medical students and professors of the University of Lisbon. When Alves met his demise in 1841, phrenology was an exciting, up-and-coming field, and Portugal’s eager phrenologists pleaded for his head to be preserved for study. By examining his skull, they believed they could determine why he killed so prolifically and ruthlessly. Did this pan out? Not really. (By 1843, phrenology was formally labeled a pseudoscience.) However, it’s a unique addition to an otherwise standard anatomical theater, sitting right next to a diaphanized hand.

This collection inside the College of Physicians has everything: 2,000 objects removed from people’s throats, conjoined twin skeletons, the remains of a 7-foot-6-inch man, and, most notably, slivers of Albert Einstein’s brain. Displayed across 46 microscope slides, these strands have been studied extensively over the years, with some scientists suggesting that Einstein’s brain architecture gave him the “combinatory play” of image he claimed was essential to his discoveries. Others look at it and see … just regular old brain matter, in less-than-ideal condition after its multiple trips across the country.

Recent findings suggest that st. Anthony was a renowned speaker during his lifetime, traveling across France and Italy preaching the word of God. Thus, it’s fitting that the one nondecomposed part of his body (exhumed in 1263) was his tongue. The saint’s tongue and jaw are now housed at his namesake basilica in Padua, displayed in ornate gold reliquaries that allow him to keep spreading the Gospel, even in death. The building itself is also a marvel, combining Romanesque, Byzantine, and Gothic architectural styles and housing artwork by Giotto and Donatello.

Before Prince René de Chalon passed away at the age of 25, he specified that he did not want his dead body to look beautiful. Au contraire: René wanted to be remembered as a rotting corpse, with dried skin flaps and a hollow carcass. His wishes were granted in this grotesque, white-stone statue inside the Church of Saint-Étienne-le-Vieux, created by Ligier Richier in 1547. The heart-shaped reliquary in the statue’s hand once held the shriveled remains of René’s own heart; however, the heart was lost (or stolen…) during the French Revolution. Nevertheless, the ghoulish artwork is a dark reminder that all of us will go from “dust to dust.”.

Sources indicate that composer Frédéric Chopin’s dying wish was that his heart be sent back to his native Poland rather than buried with the rest of his body in his adopted home of Paris. And what is family for if not to deliver on such requests? Chopin’s sister, Ludwika Jędrzejewicz, plucked out his heart before his interment, then smuggled it to Warsaw in a jar of booze. Placed beneath the city’s Holy Cross Church, the heart became a point of pride for Polish nationalists, so much so that the Nazis took it during World War II to weaken the country’s morale. (Thankfully, Germany returned it after the war.).

It has been revealed that the shoulder bone of St. Valentine was supposedly brought to the Saints Peter and Paul Basilica in the 1300s by Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV, though it was not discovered until 2002, when church members found it while organizing the basement. Ever since, the shoulder blade has been on permanent display, with a special Mass honoring it on Valentine’s Day. Since many churches have claimed parts of St. Valentine over the years, there is some doubt about the authenticity of the bone. Whether this decorated shoulder belonged to the real saint or an imposter will likely remain a mystery forever, but regardless, it’s a wonderfully weird symbol of love.

Forensic pathologist Yuri Shchukin has put his decades of morgue experience into this passion project: over 700 body parts and organs showing the ruinous effects of vice. Within his collection you’ll find such novelties as embryos from drinking and drug-taking mothers, the severed finger of an unfaithful husband, and a horn that supposedly sprouted from the head of a robber. A Latin inscription at the entrance reads: “This is a place where the dead teach the living.”.

Industry observers note that almost a century after Galileo was laid to rest, an antiquarian and an anatomist removed his middle finger, along with two other fingers and a tooth (why, exactly, is anyone’s guess). The finger was soon handed over to Florence’s Laurentian Library and, eventually, the Museo Galileo, where it is still on display today in an egg-shaped glass case with a marble base. A commemorative inscription by astronomer Tommaso Perelli reads: “Spurn not the remains of the finger by which the right hand measured out paths of the sky, pointed to orbs never before seen by mortals.” In 2009, Galileo’s middle finger had a heartwarming reunion with his newly authenticated index finger, thumb, and tooth.

When Saint Catherine died in 1380, her hometown of Siena wanted to keep her body but knew that Rome wouldn’t give it over willingly. So, the Sienese got creative: cutting off her head, putting it in a paper bag, and sneaking it past the Roman guards (praying for Catherine’s protection all the while). Upon their safe arrival back in Siena, these smugglers placed the head inside an ornate reliquary in the Basilica of San Domenico, where it remains today. Catherine’s thumb, too, is on display at the basilica, though her foot is all the way in Venice.

It has been revealed that this enormous complex in Singapore’s Chinatown was erected for a single reason: to display one of the Buddha’s chompers, supposedly recovered from a collapsed stupa in Myanmar in the 1980s. (Never mind that some experts have called the tooth “definitely not human.”) Whether you believe in the tooth’s authenticity or not, it’s worth a visit to the temple just to take in its surroundings: multiple floors of Buddha statues, dragon snakes guarding sacred relics, and a stunning front prayer hall.

This permanent exhibition inside the National Museum of Ireland is devoted to Iron and Bronze Age human sacrifices that were deposited in bogs along tribal boundaries, a.k.a. “bog bodies.” The collection includes the Cashel Man, the oldest fleshed bog body ever unearthed, as well as the Gallagh Man, who was strangled by a willow twig rope. Along with the bodies themselves, visitors can view Iron Age artifacts like horse trappings, weapons, utensils, boundary markers, and votive deposits of butter known as “bog butter.”.

Capt. Samuel Jones, a beloved tavern proprietor in rural New Hampshire, was doing construction work one day in 1804 when his leg got pinned between a building and a fence. The resulting injury was so bad that Jones had to have the leg amputated, but he did not despair. Instead, he decided to hold a funeral for his lost limb and bury it in the local cemetery, in part as a precaution against phantom limb pain. When Jones passed away years later, his body was interred elsewhere (theories range from Boston to Rhode Island to the Bronx), but his leg remains here, marked by a simple gravestone.

#106. Love with nowhere to go

📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3866 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Aeon ↗ Open Full Page

Love with nowhere to go

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive.
  • Recent findings suggest that and yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning.
  • It has been revealed that over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, I have been grieving my mother for years, even though she is still alive. Sometimes before falling asleep – in that liminal space between waking and sleeping where the self becomes porous – I’d see the image of the sweet and caring woman who would come to say goodnight, her cheeks covered in thick layers of night cream. Then, out of nowhere, the image would flip into the raging woman who was so entangled in her own suffering that she turned her frustration on us. Over the years, that second woman slowly swallowed the first, as she got pulled into my brother’s addiction. It’s hard to say where her own unhappiness ended and my brother’s suffering began, but together they drifted into a parallel reality, cut off from the world beyond their heads. There was no funeral for this. No condolence cards. No flowers. No phone calls. No leave of absence. What was I supposed to mourn?

Recent findings suggest that and yet what I felt for them, what I still feel, has the unmistakable gravity of mourning. Can there be grief without death? I have come to think that we grieve much more often than we realise, and that death is grief’s most visible occasion rather than its essence. If that doesn’t match your experience, it may be because we rarely call these other losses by their name. Most of our losses arrive without a funeral. That is the human predicament: we are creatures built to attach, living in a world where nothing stays. Sooner or later, we lose the things we care about. And since we are complex beings with a body, a mind, a community and an environment – beings who love many different things – there is a great deal we can lose, from our physical health to our sense of who we are, from relationships to homelands to the natural world we share with other species. For creatures like us, there is no way around heartbreak: to live is to lose. Grief is what love does when its object is gone. It is love with nowhere to go.

It has been revealed that over the past few years I have accumulated many such losses. There is the psychological loss of my father as I knew and loved him: a brutal stroke rendered him incapable of walking and cycling, and cycling was the only thing that could ‘make his thoughts liquid’, as he used to say. There is the loss of old friendships. First you are no longer part of each other’s lives – you just update one another about your life – and then, one day, it becomes awkward to reach out at all. There is the gradual softening of an academic identity I’d spent the most vital years of my life constructing. It was a genuine vocation, a life of the mind that taught me to think slowly and carefully. But it was also, as I came to realise, a way of living safely at one remove from where actual life takes place. What is slipping away is a future in which being an academic philosopher would be the whole answer to the question of who I am.

Recent findings suggest that there was the woman whose calmness, clarity and silence embodied the qualities I have come to like so much about the Nordics since moving to Norway. Like a magical stranger, she entered my life unexpectedly, but at the same time her arrival felt so natural, her presence so obvious, that it was as if she had always been there. After our first meeting, which lasted almost 24 hours, I wrote in my journal: Ze is gekomen om te blijven. ‘She had come to stay.’ And she did, for nine intense months. She tried to teach me to ski. We listened to the music of Nils Frahm, which reminded her of melting snow. And she made me see that the deepest form of intimacy happens in the space between the words.

According to recent reports, but despite the depth of our bond, she left, abruptly, as if she had never been there. She had fallen in love with another man. I was left behind, dazed and disoriented, and although my heart was broken, this kind of loss did not have a name that matched how shattered I felt. It was ‘just a breakup’, and it didn’t even deserve that name: we had been dating, but it never technically became a relationship. It was also a romantic connection that ran alongside another one, a long partnership that was open by mutual agreement and conscious design. Much about it wasn’t legible to most people around me. I faced the grief largely by myself. No scripts, no rituals, no recognised form, no legitimacy, no shared language, no way to make sense of what had happened to me.

Part of what made the experience so disorienting was a narrow idea of what grief is. In psychology, in philosophy and in our Western culture at large, grief has been treated almost exclusively as a response to the death of someone we love. It’s a neat, tidy understanding. The most celebrated grief memoirs – think of The Year of Magical Thinking (2005) by Joan Didion and A Grief Observed (1961) by C S Lewis – are concerned with the loss of a life partner. And Michael Cholbi’s Grief: A Philosophical Guide (2021) – one of the most extensive philosophical treatments of the emotion – focuses mostly on the grief we experience at the death of someone we love or who otherwise matters to us.

Restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches.

Sources indicate that death is visible and final: it has a body, a date, a medical certificate. The other losses are blurrier: they have no physical object, no clear beginning or end, no tangible proof they happened. We also have an infrastructure for death: funerals, condolence cards, flowers, casseroles, bereavement leave – a whole social script. Perhaps the infrastructure defines what counts: if there is no social and cultural scaffolding to digest the experience, it must not be real grief.

The prime reason for the single-minded focus on death loss, however, must be that bereavement is simply the most striking instance of a broader emotional phenomenon that comes in degrees. But restricting grief to bereavement is like restricting pain to cluster headaches, anxiety to panic attacks, sadness to depression, or pleasure to ecstasy – it is taking the most extreme instantiation of something and making it the essence of that thing.

If grief isn’t just about death, what is it about? What do all these cases of grief share? A good way to answer this question starts from the observation that every emotion has a characteristic thing it is about. Fear is about danger or threat; anger is about offence or injustice; happiness and joy are about flourishing or harmony between self and world. What is grief about? If you say ‘death’, you are doing something weird: you are defining the emotion by the particular thing that sets it off, rather than by what that thing means to us. In technical philosophical jargon, you are making the mistake of conflating an emotion’s material object with its formal object. Fear of sharks, fear of public speaking and fear of heights aren’t three different emotions – shark-fear, public-speaking-fear and heights-fear. All three count as fear because they are about danger: their aim is to tell you something is threatening.

Grief clearly has something to do with loss. Although this gets us somewhere, it doesn’t get us far enough. Mere loss is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a pen or an old sweater, I am not experiencing any grief. If I have any emotional reaction at all, it will be a slight ripple of annoyance. Perhaps we should add that for there to be grief we must lose something we care about or love, but, again, this is necessary but not sufficient. If I lose a book I really like or don’t get a dream job I applied for, what I experience is frustration or disappointment, sadness perhaps, but not grief.

What sets grief apart is how deeply the loss reaches into the fabric of your life: grief begins where your identity is disrupted. What is lost in the case of grief is not just some concrete, historical object, but a cluster of (future) possibilities that are tightly woven into your sense of identity, life structure or experiential world. When they go, you don’t just lose something: you lose a version of yourself, your life is turned upside down, and you come to inhabit, in a real sense, a different world. This is why death is grief’s most extreme instance, rather than its only one. When someone we love dies, every possibility – not only our own possibilities with them, but their possibilities too – is wiped out. As Matthew Ratcliffe and Louise Richardson, academic philosophers at the University of York, put it in their paper ‘Grief Over Non-Death Losses: A Phenomenological Perspective’ (2023):.

This reorganisation is not merely cognitive. It lives in many other places: in the body (the hand that still reaches for the phone to text someone who no longer answers your messages), in how you experience your surroundings (the café you used to visit together that now feels alien or even hostile), or in your autobiographical memories (the shared joke that simply doesn’t land with other people).

‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to’.

My mother is still alive. No one has died: there is no concrete, historical object that has been pulled beyond my grasp. But a whole set of possibilities that had been woven into the structure of my life and world, all bound up with having a mother who was present, responsive, good enough – those are gone. It has become impossible to call her and poke that mind of hers, so unusually free and unusually deep.

The same goes for my father. Sure, he survived the stroke. But the man whose restless mind needed to cycle to make his thoughts liquid – the future I had with that man, the shared cycling trips in the south of France, the conversations that needed repetitive, cyclical movement to come alive – that future was negated. The same structure holds for the woman whose disappearance collapsed an experiential world that felt like a home I had only just found, and for the academic identity I had built over almost two decades. As other vocations began to call more insistently, a single, all-consuming way of being in the world – the thinker, the life of the mind, the person whose future would be organised around reading and writing – loosened its hold.

It has been revealed that the case that makes this way of thinking about grief most compelling, though, is one where there is no concrete object of loss at all. Ratcliffe and Richardson’s central example is involuntary childlessness – grief for a child who never was, a future that was imagined, anticipated and deeply woven into one’s sense of self, but that never materialised. Here, no one died and no one left. There is nothing tangible to point to: no grave, no anniversary, no recorded name, no memorial service, no shared practices to give words or meaning to the loss. And yet, as one respondent in their study put it: ‘No one can understand what it’s like to carry this loss. In their minds, no baby meant no loss.’ Another respondent simply called their grief by its name: ‘I am grieving the future children I imagined and believed I would have but am unable to.’ And a third spoke, chillingly, of ‘the death of a future life’.

They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience.

Sources indicate that ‘No baby meant no loss.’ Many forms of non-death loss are what the family therapist Pauline Boss calls ‘ambiguous loss’. These are losses without clear boundaries, without a definite beginning or end – cases where someone is physically present but psychologically gone, or physically gone but psychologically still there. Think of an Alzheimer’s patient whose self has been erased by the disease or of a soldier missing in action. Because many non-death losses are ambiguous, the grief that follows them is not openly acknowledged, socially validated or publicly mourned – what the grief scholar Kenneth Doka has called ‘disenfranchised grief’.

In a recent development, those whose grief is disenfranchised because their losses are ambiguous don’t just lack scripts or rituals or traditions. They lack the interpretative resources to understand and share significant aspects of their experience. When we lack the concepts to name what it is like to be us, what it is we are going through, we suffer what the philosopher Miranda Fricker calls a ‘hermeneutical injustice’ – an inability to make our own experience intelligible to ourselves and to others. This is not because we are confused, but because the shared language or conceptual apparatus – the frameworks we use to make sense of ourselves – hasn’t caught up. As two of Ratcliffe and Richardson’s respondents put it: ‘It took me a while to understand that what I was feeling was grief’; ‘I never realised this was grief until I found others in a similar situation.’.

The same happened to me: when the magical stranger disappeared, my loss was ambiguous – she still existed, we were never officially together, I had another partner – and my grief went into hiding. In a culture where the end of a relationship is ‘just a breakup’ and monogamy is the unspoken rule, I lacked the rituals to digest the grief and the hermeneutical resources to conceptualise and communicate what had happened to me. For ‘self-interpreting animals’ like us, in the words of the philosopher Charles Taylor, the result is that we end up in the dark, as strangers to ourselves.

The narrowing of grief to bereavement is more than a conceptual mistake. It does real damage. What the writer and grief counsellor Stephen Levine called ‘unattended sorrow’ doesn’t dissolve but goes underground, hiding in the shadows, later resurfacing as unexpected symptoms. I have been there. A mechanical tightness in the chest and a hard belly, like wearing a harness to brace against life. Harrowing dreams. Attempts to numb what is too painful to feel alone. And, worst of all, cynicism and a slow erosion of trust. Not just in other people, but in your own feelings, your own intuitions about the depth, sustainability and future of any new connection. When no one around you recognises your grief, you begin to wonder whether you were wrong to feel it at all.

Industry observers note that sigmund Freud understood this, though he read it as pathology. In the essay ‘Mourning and Melancholia’ (1917), he contended that grief is healthy and normal, but only if it is intelligible and bounded. The job of mourning, he argued, is to detach you from the lost object and reinvest your emotional energy elsewhere. If you can’t complete that job, if the loss is unclear or unnamed or ambiguous, you are no longer mourning. Instead, you are suffering from an illness called melancholia. For Freud, grief that cannot do its work calcifies into something darker, something more elusive.

If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to themselves.

But the damage runs deeper than that. When we cannot grieve a loss, we lose something else along with it: the chance to register what mattered to us. Grief is how we come to know what we loved in the presence of its absence. Or as the psychotherapist and grief worker Francis Weller puts it in The Wild Edge of Sorrow (2015):.

Your grief tells you that you had the courage to love, that you allowed someone or something else to enter ‘the core of [your] being and find a home in [your] heart’. If you deny someone the right to grieve, you deny them access to what they loved and valued, which is to say that you deny them access to themselves. You don’t just rob them, then, of their love; you also rob them of self-knowledge.

Sources indicate that the tradition I spent most of my life in – the lineage of Western thinkers who asked how a human being should live – was the first place I looked to understand what was happening to me. These thinkers had a lot to say about grief, but most of it was suspicious and sceptical. Plato believed a good man is the most self-sufficient of all, and least shaken by loss. In the Phaedo, Socrates’ wife Xanthippe is led away wailing before the philosophy can begin, and towards the end of the dialogue, Socrates rebukes his weeping friends for behaving like women. A similar sentiment can be found among the Stoics. Epictetus, in the Enchiridion, compares the loss of a wife or child to a jug breaking. And Marcus Aurelius, who lost many of his own children, reminds himself in his Meditations not to pray that he might keep his child, but to pray that he might not fear losing him.

Sources indicate that behind this way of thinking lies an expensive belief: that attachment is a liability, and that a wise person – someone who has figured out how to live the best possible life – does not need anything that can be taken away from him. If grief is love with nowhere to go, a tradition that treated such love as an error was never going to know what to do with it.

Industry observers note that christianity kept the verdict the ancients had arrived at. In his Confessions (397-400 CE), Saint Augustine looks back on his devastation after a friend’s death, and diagnoses it as a spiritual mistake: ‘Why had that grief penetrated me so easily and so deeply, if not because I had poured out my soul onto the sand, loving someone who would die as if he never would?’ Baruch Spinoza – not religious in any conventional sense of the word – reached the same conclusion. Sadness, he writes in his Ethics (1677), is the mind’s move to a lesser perfection, a loss of its power to act. This means it can never be a good in itself, and its typical source is too much love for things that are impermanent. The cure for grief – and this puts him squarely back into the ancient intellectualist tradition – is understanding: the moment it dawns on us that what we lost could never have been kept, our grief will relax.

The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most crucial manual as a mark of disorder.

In a recent development, arthur Schopenhauer, unlike many before him, did not despise grief. In The World as Will and Representation (1818), he values sorrow for one reason only: great personal suffering breaks the will and leads to self-renunciation (Selbstverneinung). Grief is worth having, then, because it has the power to cure us of wanting the world at all, which means that, in the end, he is not so far from the thinkers who came before him. A good life, for all of them, is a matter of loosening our attachments to what is impermanent and fragile.

What began as a doctrine of philosophers leaked into the wider culture. In his landmark study Death, Grief, and Mourning in Contemporary Britain (1965), the anthropologist Geoffrey Gorer found that mourning was increasingly seen as ‘a weakness, a self-indulgence, a reprehensible bad habit instead of as a psychological necessity’. In the 1970s, the historian Philippe Ariès traced the same shift across the industrial West: death, once familiar, had become shameful, something to be hidden. Meanwhile, medicine had entered the debate. In 1961, the psychiatrist George Engel asked, half provocatively, whether grief was a disease. In 2000, the philosopher Stephen Wilkinson answered: yes. In one of academic philosophy’s leading journals, he argued that even normal, healthy grief qualifies as a mental disorder because it meets the standard definition of one. Like all mental disorders, it involves significant distress and interrupts normal functioning. In 2013, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders removed the clause that had excluded the recently bereaved from receiving a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. Then, in 2022, the revised edition added prolonged grief disorder, whose possible symptoms include identity disruption, such as the feeling that part of oneself has died. The sense that part of oneself has been lost now appears in psychiatry’s most important manual as a mark of disorder – though, tellingly, only when someone has actually died.

Sources indicate that but the Western tradition had it backwards. Suppressing, eradicating, denying or pathologising grief doesn’t protect the good life; it sabotages human flourishing by cutting us off from the things we love. More than that, it cuts us off from each other. Grief named and disclosed is grief that can be met, grief that can be placed between you and another person, where the two of you can look at it and hold it together. That shared vulnerability lets one person recognise another in their common humanity. Grief, as Weller reminds us, was never meant to be carried alone; it was meant to be held and processed by a whole village. Strip it of its name and you strip people of the possibility of being seen in their loss, of discovering that the wound they thought was theirs alone is in fact shared by those around them.

Recently, while in the Netherlands, I visited the Kröller-Müller Museum with my father, the same father whose future was negated by a stroke. I looked at him from a distance, the man who once built his life around cycling – to France, to Rome, to Spain’s Santiago de Compostela – now hunched behind his rollator. We stood together in front of Vincent van Gogh’s painting At Eternity’s Gate (1890): an old man, face buried in his fists, clearly hurting. A sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man, looking at a sorrowful man painted by a sorrowful man. Years before he painted it, when he first drew the same figure for a lithograph, Van Gogh wrote that there can be an ‘unutterably moving’ quality, ‘something precious, something noble’, in the expression of an old man like that.

In a recent development, at Eternity’s Gate (1890) by Vincent van Gogh. Courtesy the Kröller-Müller Museum, Netherlands.

I didn’t know my father loved Van Gogh as much as I do. We stood there for a long time – somehow in contact with the magic of grief – and something opened up between us that had no name but felt important, exquisitely alive. We didn’t talk about my mother, or how our family had unravelled, or what the stroke had taken from him. We didn’t have to. The painting stated what neither of us could.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For thousands of years, ancient Egyptian was spoken along the Nile, and plenty of its words got out. Greek traders and Roman writers picked some of them up; Arabic and Spanish passed others along; and a handful made it all the way into English, where most people use them without a second thought. Here are nine words that are believed to have started out in Egypt. Some of these trails are well marked, and some run cold partway back, so etymologists hedge a few of them.

The word paper reached English in the mid-14th century, by way of Old French papier, from the Latin papyrus, the reed that gave the Ancient Egyptians a cheap, convenient writing surface. The Greeks called the plant papyros, and the Online Etymology Dictionary calls that a loanword of unknown origin that is âoften said to be Egyptian.â So the trail runs from the Nile to your printer tray, with one smudged signpost in the middle.

Egyptian had a word, hbnj, for a dark, hard wood prized for carving, and itâs probably where the Greeks got ebenos. From there the Romans made it ebenus, and English took ebony in the 1590s. Writers were using it to mean a vary dark black color by the 1620s, which is why a word for lumber now reveals up in poetry, piano lessons, and paint-chip names.

Before English borrowed ivory from French in the 13th century, Old English speakers called the stuff elpendban, or âelephant bone.â The newer word traces back to the Latin ebur, which the Online Etymology Dictionary claims likely came from an African source by way of Phoenician, and it points to the Egyptian ab, âelephant,â and the Coptic ebu, âivory.â By 1782, ivories was slang for teeth, and by 1818 it meant piano keys.

The sun-dried brick of the American Southwest has an Egyptian name. English got adobe from Spanish in 1739, and the 19th-century Dutch Arabist Reinhart Dozy traced the Spanish word to the Arabic al-tob, âthe brick.â Before that it was the Coptic tobe, from an ancient Egyptian word for brick, á¸bt, that turns up in hieroglyphics.

A competing theory ties adobe to the Spanish verb adobar, âto plaster,â but if Dozy was right, a mud brick in New Mexico still answers to roughly the name it had on the Nile.

English got oasis through Latin from the Greek Oasis, and behind the Greek is the Egyptian wá¸¥ê£t, which, according to Raymond Faulknerâs dictionary of Middle Egyptian, could mean both âoasisâ and âcauldron.â The word passed through a later stage of Egyptian on its way to the Greeks, and its cousins survive in Coptic as ouahe and in Arabic as wÄá¸¥a.

The sticky stuff that seeps out of trees went from the Egyptian qmyt, a word for resin, to the Greek kommi, to the Latin gummi, and on into Middle English. Chewing gum came much later and simply inherited the name. The gums in your mouth are a different word entirely, from the Old English gÅma, âpalate,â so only half of the gum you have right now is Egyptian.

Sources indicate that greek had a word, baris, for a specifically Egyptian kind of boat, borrowed from Egyptian (Coptic bari, âsmall boatâ). The Online Etymology Dictionary calls the next step uncertain, but a likely route runs through Latin and Old French to give English barge in the early 14th century. Its relatives bark and barque may share the same Nile ancestor. The sense of barging into a room, from the rough way barges got handled, dates only to 1898.

Recent findings suggest that hereâs one for the cleaning cabinet. The ancient Greeks and Romans worshipped the Egyptian god Amun as Ammon, whose name is stated to mean âhidden,â and he had an oracle at a desert shrine in what they called Libya. Mineral salts gathered near it came to be called sal ammoniac, Ammonâs salt, and in 1782 the Swedish chemist Torbern Bergman coined ammonia for the gas made from it.

The etymologist Joseph Shipley wrote that the salts traditionally came âfrom the sands where the camels waited while their masters prayed for good omens.â.

This is the most debated word on the list. Chemistry was used to mean alchemy around 1600, and alchemy goes back through Arabic al-kimiya to a Greek word that turns up around 300 CE in a decree by the Roman emperor Diocletian against âthe old writings of the Egyptians.â One theory traces it to Khemia, an old name for Egypt that means âland of black earth.â The other links it to a Greek word for pouring.

The Online Etymology Dictionaryâs verdict is that the word âseems to have elements of both origins,â so Egypt gets at least partial credit.

The Amarna letters

📅 28 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (140 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Aeon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that first discovered in Egypt in the late 19th century, the collection of clay tablets known as the Amarna letters is one of our richest windows into the ancient world. The letters are extraordinary not only for their contents – diplomatic communications exchanged between Egyptian pharaohs and other nearby rulers in the 14th century BCE – but also for their script: they were written not in Egyptian hieroglyphs but largely in cuneiform, a writing system most often associated with ancient Mesopotamia. In this video from the British Museum, the always entertaining Assyriologist Irving Finkel details how the letters came to be and how they were discovered, and delves into the fascinating correspondence itself, which includes petty disputes over perceived slights, leaders lobbying for military support and more than a few requests for gold.

If the specifics seem hard to picture, I think that might be the point. Baraghani has thrived historically by taking a straightforward-seeming dish and twisting it just off-kilter, so it is a few degrees punchier and much more beautiful than you were expecting. The result is food that is as much about the people and places evoked by the flavors as it is about aesthetic provocation. (That Italian Stallion shirt, he tells me, is long gone.).

Literally speaking, Ditto will be a revival of the sort of counter-service restaurant Baraghani has long adored, from Gjusta in Los Angeles to City Bakery in New York. He and Silber sprang for a shiny rotisserie oven, for what they’re calling a “beyond chicken program,” with plans for spit-roasted porchetta, romanesco, and cabbage.

According to recent reports, the goal is dishes that are palpably human, in a space Baraghani hopes will seem accessible to everyone. It was key for both owners to find a space in a hub neighborhood. With the storefront they chose, a former Agnès B. on 16th Street, Greenmarket shoppers can stop by for a selection of California-ish sides and salads displayed Yotam Ottolenghi–style, counter pastries, or just to peruse marketplace provisions: tahini, harissa, dates (and, for now, no tinned fish). Maybe, one day, they’ll stay open for dinner service, but for now the initiative is breakfast and lunch.

Suddenly Baraghani is moving again, reaching for his phone to show me a photo of a dish he would have loved to serve, had Con Ed turned on the gas in time for a September opening: a mound of spicy tuna salad piled perkily in a blanched tomato with a turret of scallion greens.

The sight makes me hungry, and I realize we still haven’t gone out for that cream. Ninety minutes have passed and I have yet to ask any of the questions I’d prepared for Baraghani, who keeps surprising me with disclosures. (Such as: He did not speak until he was three years old.).

Suddenly, it is time to head to Ditto for a tour, cream and scones be damned.

As we walk over, I ask about the restaurant’s name. He asks if I’ve seen the movie Ghost. I have, but not for a while. “It’s another way to say ‘I love you,’” he says simply, before disappearing to join a meeting.

Later I dig up that scene Baraghani mentioned and press play. In it, Whoopi Goldberg tries to convince a frustrated Demi Moore that her recently deceased boyfriend has returned as a ghost. Moore jumps up in disbelief to flee the restaurant as Patrick Swayze, the boyfriend, scrambles to find a way to prove to her that he’s right there. “Tell her ‘ditto,’” he urges Goldberg, who screams “ditto” after Moore as she bolts. “Ditto!” It’s their code word for “I love you too.”.

Moore stops in her tracks and turns, her gaze connecting with a man she misses, who she isn’t totally sure is there.

In a recent development, and for the first time in a while, she is no longer in motion. She is still.

Their scheme was discovered and stopped in early November of that year, and has gone down as one of the most notorious murder cases in Scottish history.

Industry observers note that in 1836, a group of boys were exploring a cave on Arthurâs Seatâa prominent hill in Edinburghâwhen they found 17 tiny coffins that contained strange dolls. #99. The physics of getting fired
